guides.title: The B Vitamins and Their Functions
guides.summary: What each of the eight B vitamins does inside the body, the coenzymes they become, and how deficiency of each one presents. Covers food sources and cooking losses, fortification, safe upper limits, the genuine toxicities, and the interactions that matter clinically.

sections.heading: What the B Vitamins Are and Why They Are Grouped Together
sections.body: The B vitamins are eight distinct chemical substances that have almost nothing in common structurally and are grouped together for reasons that are half historical accident and half genuine biology. They are thiamin, sometimes written thiamine, numbered B1; riboflavin, B2; niacin, B3; pantothenic acid, B5; vitamin B6, which is a family of six related compounds; biotin, B7; folate, B9; and cobalamin, B12. The gaps in the numbering are real and are worth explaining, because they are the origin of a great deal of supplement marketing nonsense. The grouping began with a mistake. In the early twentieth century researchers separating the newly discovered accessory food factors found that one fraction dissolved in fat and another in water, and named them fat soluble A and water soluble B. The Polish biochemist Casimir Funk coined the word vitamine in 1912 for the substance in rice bran that cured beriberi. It soon emerged that water soluble B was not one substance at all. Heating destroyed part of its activity and left part intact, so the heat labile fraction was called B1 and the heat stable one B2, and as separation techniques improved the list kept growing. Numbers were assigned as candidates appeared, and several were later withdrawn when the substance turned out not to be essential for humans, which is why the sequence has holes at four, eight, ten, eleven and beyond. There is nevertheless a real biological reason to treat them as a family. All eight are water soluble, so with one striking exception the body stores very little of them and a continuing dietary supply is needed. All eight work by being converted into coenzymes, the small non protein helper molecules that many enzymes require in order to catalyse their reactions at all. And they overlap heavily in the foods that supply them, so that the classic B vitamin sources, liver, whole grains, legumes, eggs, dairy and yeast, deliver most of them at once. That overlap is why deficiency of a single B vitamin in isolation is unusual outside of specific medical situations, and why real world deficiency usually presents as a blurred multi vitamin picture. The exception to the storage rule is vitamin B12, of which the liver holds two to five milligrams, several years' worth at a requirement of a few micrograms a day. Folate stores of perhaps five to twenty milligrams last a few months. Thiamin stores last only two to three weeks, which is why thiamin deficiency can develop alarmingly fast in someone who stops eating. Understanding those three timescales explains most of the clinical urgency in this whole subject: a person who has eaten nothing for a fortnight needs thiamin before anything else, while a person who has eaten no animal food for two years may still be entirely well and only becoming deficient in B12 now.

sections.heading: Coenzymes: The Shared Mechanism Behind Every B Vitamin
sections.body: Almost every enzyme in the body is a protein, and proteins are made of twenty amino acids whose chemical range is limited. There are reactions that no combination of those twenty side chains can perform: transferring a hydride ion, carrying an activated acetyl group, shuttling a single carbon atom, rearranging a carbon skeleton. For these, enzymes recruit help in the form of a coenzyme, a small non protein molecule that supplies the missing chemistry. The great majority of coenzymes in human metabolism are made from B vitamins, and this single fact explains nearly everything about how they behave. The conversion from vitamin to coenzyme is usually a small chemical modification. Thiamin is pyrophosphorylated to thiamin pyrophosphate. Riboflavin becomes flavin mononucleotide and then flavin adenine dinucleotide. Niacin is built into nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide. Pantothenic acid becomes part of coenzyme A. Vitamin B6 is phosphorylated and oxidised to pyridoxal 5 phosphate. Folate is reduced to tetrahydrofolate. Biotin is attached covalently to its enzyme, and cobalamin acquires either a methyl or an adenosyl group. In each case the vitamin is the part the body cannot build from scratch, and the rest of the coenzyme is assembled around it. Three consequences follow directly. First, the amounts required are tiny, measured in milligrams or even micrograms per day, because a coenzyme is a catalyst that is used and regenerated many times rather than consumed. A person needs perhaps 2.4 micrograms of B12 daily, an amount you could not see. Second, deficiency symptoms are diffuse and multisystem rather than specific, because a coenzyme used by dozens of enzymes fails in dozens of places at once. This is why the classic deficiency syndromes all involve some mixture of skin, mouth, gut, blood and nerve, and why they are so easily mistaken for one another or for unrelated illness. Third, the tissues that fail first are those with the highest turnover and the greatest metabolic demand: the lining of the mouth and gut, which renews itself every few days; the bone marrow, which produces around two million red cells a second; the skin; and nerve tissue, which cannot be replaced at all and therefore accumulates damage. That last point carries the most important practical implication in the whole subject. Damage to epithelium and blood recovers within days or weeks of correcting the deficiency, while damage to peripheral nerves and spinal cord may recover only partially or not at all. Delay in treating a B vitamin deficiency that has reached the nervous system converts a reversible condition into a permanent disability, which is the reason clinicians treat suspected thiamin and B12 deficiency urgently rather than waiting for confirmatory tests. It also explains a persistent piece of misunderstanding. Because these coenzymes sit in the pathways that release energy from food, supplements are marketed as though they supply energy themselves. They do not. They permit the extraction of energy from the calories you eat, and in a person who already has enough, adding more changes nothing at all.

sections.heading: Thiamin: The Gateway to Burning Sugar
sections.body: Thiamin becomes thiamin pyrophosphate, a coenzyme required by a small number of enzymes that happen to sit at metabolic choke points. The most important is the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, which converts pyruvate, the end product of glycolysis, into acetyl coenzyme A so that it can enter the citric acid cycle. Without thiamin pyrophosphate that step stops, and the cell cannot extract more than a small fraction of the energy in glucose. A second enzyme, alpha ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, sits inside the citric acid cycle itself. A third, transketolase, operates in the pentose phosphate pathway, which supplies the ribose used to build nucleic acids and the reducing power used to defend against oxidative damage. Because red blood cell transketolase activity responds sensitively to thiamin supply, measuring it is a classic laboratory test of thiamin status. Tissues that depend heavily on glucose suffer first and worst, which means the brain, the peripheral nerves and the heart. Deficiency produces beriberi, a disease known in two main forms. Wet beriberi affects the cardiovascular system, producing a high output heart failure with rapid pulse, breathlessness and swelling of the legs. Dry beriberi produces a symmetrical peripheral neuropathy with numbness, burning feet, weakness and wasting. In the brain, acute deficiency causes Wernicke encephalopathy, a medical emergency classically described as confusion, unsteadiness and abnormal eye movements, although all three appear together in only a minority of cases, so the absence of the full triad must never be used to rule it out. Untreated, it can progress to Korsakoff syndrome, a permanent inability to form new memories, often with confabulation. The historical route to understanding it is instructive. Beriberi became epidemic in east and southeast Asia in the nineteenth century as steam powered milling made polished white rice cheap, stripping away the bran and germ where the thiamin lies. Takaki Kanehiro nearly eliminated it from the Japanese navy in the 1880s by changing rations. Christiaan Eijkman, working in Java in the 1890s, produced the same disease in chickens fed polished rice and cured it with the discarded bran, work for which he shared the Nobel Prize in 1929. Two practical points matter more than any other. Body stores amount to only about twenty five to thirty milligrams, enough for two to three weeks, so deficiency develops quickly in anyone not eating, and chronic heavy alcohol use impairs intake, absorption and activation simultaneously. And giving glucose to a thiamin depleted person consumes their last reserves and can precipitate acute Wernicke encephalopathy. Thiamin must therefore be given before or alongside intravenous glucose in anyone at risk, a rule that has saved a great many people from permanent brain injury. The same logic applies to refeeding after prolonged starvation and to severe vomiting in pregnancy. Recommended intakes are modest, about 1.2 milligrams a day for men and 1.1 for women, and no upper limit has been set because oral thiamin has no meaningful toxicity, so there is nothing to lose by giving it when in doubt.

sections.heading: Riboflavin: The Vitamin That Other Vitamins Depend On
sections.body: Riboflavin becomes two closely related coenzymes, flavin mononucleotide and flavin adenine dinucleotide, known as FMN and FAD. Both are electron carriers, and unlike most such carriers they can accept electrons either singly or in pairs, which makes them uniquely versatile and places them at junctions where different kinds of chemistry meet. FMN sits inside complex one of the mitochondrial respiratory chain, the entry point for most of the electrons that ultimately produce cellular energy. FAD is the working part of succinate dehydrogenase, which belongs simultaneously to the citric acid cycle and to the respiratory chain, and of the acyl coenzyme A dehydrogenases that begin the breakdown of fatty acids. FAD also drives glutathione reductase, the enzyme that regenerates the cell's main antioxidant defence, and the responsiveness of that enzyme in red cells to added riboflavin is the standard laboratory measure of riboflavin status. What makes riboflavin unusual is that several other B vitamins cannot function without it. Converting vitamin B6 into its active coenzyme requires an FMN dependent enzyme. The folate pathway enzyme methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase uses FAD. Making niacin from the amino acid tryptophan requires riboflavin at more than one step. A person short of riboflavin therefore develops functional insufficiency of B6, folate and niacin even with adequate intakes of those vitamins, which is one of the clearest illustrations of why nutrient deficiencies rarely stay tidy. Deficiency produces a recognisable cluster affecting rapidly renewing tissue: cracks and inflammation at the corners of the mouth, a sore magenta coloured tongue, greasy scaling around the nose and ears, sore and light sensitive eyes, and in prolonged cases a normal sized cell anaemia. None of these is specific, and riboflavin deficiency in the developed world is usually part of a broader poor diet. Riboflavin is chemically distinctive in two ways worth knowing in a kitchen. It is remarkably stable to heat, so cooking destroys little of it directly, and the main loss is by leaching into cooking water. But it is destroyed rapidly by light. Milk left in a clear glass bottle in sunlight can lose more than half its riboflavin within a couple of hours, which is the practical reason milk is sold in opaque cartons and plastic rather than glass. The name comes from the Latin for yellow, and the vitamin is intensely coloured and fluorescent, which is why taking a B complex supplement turns urine a startling greenish yellow within an hour or two. That effect is harmless and is simply the excess being excreted. Recommended intakes are around 1.3 milligrams a day for men and 1.1 for women, and no upper limit has been established because no toxicity has been demonstrated. Doses around four hundred milligrams a day have been studied for preventing migraine, with mixed but not negligible results.

sections.heading: Niacin, NAD and the Redox Currency of the Cell
sections.body: Niacin is the collective name for nicotinic acid and nicotinamide, two forms that the body converts into nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, universally abbreviated NAD, and its phosphorylated relative NADP. These are the most heavily used coenzymes in the whole of metabolism. NAD accepts electrons in the breakdown reactions of glycolysis, the citric acid cycle and fatty acid oxidation, and delivers them to the respiratory chain, so essentially every calorie you burn passes through it. NADP does the opposite job, supplying electrons for building things: fatty acids, cholesterol, steroid hormones, and the regeneration of antioxidants. The two forms differ by a single phosphate group, and that small difference lets the cell run its breakdown and its building economies independently. NAD is also consumed rather than merely recycled, which distinguishes it from most coenzymes. Enzymes that repair DNA breaks, the sirtuin family that removes acetyl groups from proteins, and several signalling enzymes all cleave NAD and use a fragment, so the pool must be continually rebuilt. The body can make niacin from the amino acid tryptophan, at a conversion ratio of roughly sixty milligrams of tryptophan to one milligram of niacin, which is why intakes are expressed in niacin equivalents that combine both sources. The conversion itself requires riboflavin, vitamin B6 and iron, so shortages of those can produce niacin deficiency in someone whose niacin intake looks adequate. Deficiency causes pellagra, remembered by its four Ds: dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia and death. The rash is unmistakable because it appears only on sun exposed skin, symmetrically, often forming a collar around the neck. The mechanism behind its historical geography is one of the most satisfying stories in nutrition. Maize contains niacin in a chemically bound form the gut cannot release. Mesoamerican cultures had for millennia treated maize with wood ash or slaked lime before grinding it, a process called nixtamalization, which frees the niacin. When maize spread to Europe, Africa and the American South as a crop without the accompanying technique, pellagra followed it. Joseph Goldberger demonstrated between 1914 and the 1920s that the disease in the American South was dietary rather than infectious, and Conrad Elvehjem identified nicotinamide as the curative factor in 1937. Niacin is the one B vitamin with a firm upper limit for ordinary people, set at thirty five milligrams a day from supplements and fortified food. Nicotinic acid at gram doses causes intense flushing of the skin through prostaglandin release, and in sustained release form can damage the liver. It was used for decades as a cholesterol drug, but large trials published in 2011 and 2014 found no cardiovascular benefit when added to statins, along with real harms, and that use has largely been abandoned.

sections.heading: Pantothenic Acid and Coenzyme A
sections.body: Pantothenic acid takes its name from the Greek pantothen, meaning from everywhere, and the name is the most useful thing to know about it. It is present in virtually every food of plant or animal origin, deficiency in people eating any ordinary diet is essentially unknown, and consequently it is the B vitamin that receives the least attention despite being incorporated into arguably the single most important small molecule in metabolism. That molecule is coenzyme A. Its job is to carry acyl groups, fragments of carbon chains, in an activated form that can be transferred to other molecules. The most famous of these is acetyl coenzyme A, the two carbon unit that sits at the exact centre of metabolism. Sugars broken down by glycolysis arrive as acetyl coenzyme A. Fatty acids broken down by beta oxidation arrive as acetyl coenzyme A. Many amino acids converge on it too. From that hub, carbon either enters the citric acid cycle to be burned for energy, or is built up into fatty acids, cholesterol and everything made from cholesterol, including the steroid hormones and bile acids, or is converted into ketone bodies during fasting. Acetyl coenzyme A also supplies the acetyl group for the neurotransmitter acetylcholine and for the acetylation of proteins, including the histones around which DNA is wound, which is one of the main ways gene activity is regulated. A closely related fragment of pantothenic acid, phosphopantetheine, is attached to the acyl carrier protein within fatty acid synthase, where it acts as a swinging arm passing the growing fatty acid chain from one catalytic site to the next. Between coenzyme A and the acyl carrier protein, pantothenic acid participates in something like a hundred distinct reactions. Because dietary deficiency essentially does not occur naturally, what is known about its symptoms comes from deliberate experiments using antagonists and from a small number of extreme historical situations. Prisoners of war in the Far East during the Second World War, on grossly deficient rations, described a syndrome of burning, painful feet that was attributed to pantothenic acid lack. Experimental depletion produces fatigue, irritability, numbness and impaired coordination, all of which resolve on replacement. The adequate intake for adults is set at about five milligrams a day, an amount easily obtained. No upper limit has been established, and very large doses produce nothing worse than diarrhoea. Supplements are widely sold on claims about stress and adrenal function that do not have good evidence behind them. A genetic disorder of the pathway that builds coenzyme A causes a serious neurodegenerative disease, but that is a defect of the enzyme rather than a shortage of the vitamin and does not respond to eating more of it.

sections.heading: Vitamin B6: The Amino Acid Vitamin and Its Real Toxicity
sections.body: Vitamin B6 is not one compound but six related ones, of which the body's working form is pyridoxal 5 phosphate. More enzymes depend on it than on any other coenzyme in human biology, well over a hundred distinct catalytic activities, amounting to something like four per cent of all classified enzymes. Nearly all of them act on amino acids, and they can do so because of one chemical trick. Pyridoxal 5 phosphate reacts with the amino group of an amino acid to form a temporary linkage that pulls electrons away from the neighbouring carbon, stabilising an otherwise impossibly unstable intermediate. Once that intermediate exists, several different bonds become breakable, which is why a single coenzyme supports reactions as varied as transferring an amino group, removing a carboxyl group and rearranging a side chain. The consequences reach across the body. Transamination reactions, catalysed by the enzymes whose blood levels are measured in liver function tests, move nitrogen between amino acids and allow the carbon skeletons to be burned or converted into glucose. Decarboxylation reactions produce neurotransmitters: serotonin, dopamine, gamma aminobutyric acid and histamine are all made by pyridoxal 5 phosphate dependent enzymes. The transsulfuration pathway, which disposes of the amino acid homocysteine by converting it into cysteine, needs it at two consecutive steps. The rate limiting enzyme of haem synthesis needs it, so deficiency can cause an anaemia with small pale cells and iron laden marrow precursors. Glycogen breakdown needs it, and in fact a large share of the body's total store is bound up in the glycogen phosphorylase of muscle. And the conversion of tryptophan into niacin needs it, so B6 deficiency can produce a pellagra like picture. Dietary deficiency alone is uncommon; drug induced deficiency is not. Isoniazid, used against tuberculosis, chemically inactivates pyridoxal and causes a peripheral neuropathy unless pyridoxine is given alongside it, conventionally ten to fifty milligrams a day. Cycloserine, penicillamine and hydralazine act similarly. A well documented episode in the early 1950s, in which a manufacturing change overheated an infant formula and destroyed its B6, produced convulsions in babies and established beyond doubt how quickly the deficient brain becomes unstable. Vitamin B6 also carries the clearest toxicity of any B vitamin, and it is not obscure. Prolonged high doses cause a sensory peripheral neuropathy: numbness and tingling in the hands and feet, loss of position and vibration sense, and an unsteady gait, with muscle strength preserved. The classic report of 1983 described patients taking two to six grams daily, but cases have accumulated at far lower chronic intakes, including in the low hundreds of milligrams and occasionally below. Recovery after stopping is usual but slow and sometimes incomplete. The upper limit for adults is set at one hundred milligrams a day, and doses well above that are routinely sold in nerve and energy formulations.

sections.heading: Biotin, Carboxylation and the Laboratory Test Problem
sections.body: Biotin is the coenzyme for a small, precisely defined set of five enzymes in humans, all of which do the same chemical job: attaching a carbon dioxide molecule to a target to create a new carbon to carbon bond. Biotin is not merely borrowed for these reactions but covalently bonded to its enzymes by a dedicated attaching enzyme and later released for reuse by another called biotinidase, so the vitamin circulates through a genuine recycling system. The five reactions matter more than their number suggests. Pyruvate carboxylase adds carbon dioxide to pyruvate, producing oxaloacetate, which is both the starting material for making glucose during fasting and the molecule that replenishes the citric acid cycle when its intermediates are drained off for other purposes. Acetyl coenzyme A carboxylase, in two forms, produces malonyl coenzyme A, the building block of fatty acid synthesis and simultaneously the signal that switches off fat burning, so it sits at the switch between storing and consuming fat. Propionyl coenzyme A carboxylase handles the breakdown products of odd chain fatty acids and several amino acids, and 3 methylcrotonyl coenzyme A carboxylase handles leucine. Deficiency is genuinely rare and its causes are specific. The best known is prolonged consumption of raw egg white, which contains avidin, a protein that binds biotin more tightly than almost any other non covalent interaction known in biology and carries it out of the body undigested. Cooking denatures avidin completely, so the risk applies only to people eating substantial quantities of raw whites over months. Long term treatment with certain older anticonvulsants, chronic dialysis, and an inherited deficiency of the recycling enzyme biotinidase are the other routes; the last is screened for in newborns in many countries because it responds completely to oral biotin. Symptoms include a scaly red rash around the eyes, nose and mouth, hair loss, and neurological changes ranging from lethargy to seizures. The adequate intake is thirty micrograms a day and no upper limit has been set. The reason biotin nonetheless demands attention is not nutritional but laboratory. Enormous numbers of blood tests are built on the extraordinarily strong binding between biotin and the protein streptavidin, and high dose supplements flood that system. The effect is systematic: in one common assay design results come back falsely low, and in another falsely high. That produces a thyroid pattern imitating an overactive gland, and, far more dangerously, a falsely low troponin that can hide a heart attack. Safety warnings were issued by the United States regulator in 2017 and again in 2019 following a reported death. Hair and nail supplements commonly contain five to ten thousand micrograms, hundreds of times the requirement, on evidence that is weak in anyone who is not actually deficient. Stop them at least two to three days before blood tests and tell whoever ordered them.

sections.heading: Folate, One-Carbon Metabolism and the Neural Tube
sections.body: Folate takes its name from the Latin for leaf, having first been isolated from spinach in 1941. In the body it is reduced to tetrahydrofolate, whose function is to carry single carbon atoms from where they are generated to where they are needed, holding them at whichever level of oxidation the receiving reaction requires. That sounds abstract and is in fact the foundation of cell division. Three destinations account for most of the traffic. The first is the manufacture of thymidine, one of the four bases of DNA, which is made by transferring a carbon from folate onto a uracil nucleotide. Without folate that reaction fails, uracil is mistakenly incorporated into DNA in its place, and the repair machinery cuts it out repeatedly, fragmenting the strand. The second is the construction of the purine bases adenine and guanine, which requires two separate folate dependent carbon transfers. The third is the conversion of the amino acid homocysteine back into methionine, from which the cell makes S adenosylmethionine, the universal methyl donor used to methylate DNA, RNA, proteins, phospholipids and neurotransmitters. Because DNA synthesis fails first in the tissues that divide fastest, the signature of deficiency is megaloblastic anaemia. The bone marrow keeps growing cells that cannot finish replicating their DNA, so they become abnormally large and are destroyed before release; the blood film shows oversized red cells and neutrophils with too many nuclear lobes. A sore tongue, mouth ulcers, diarrhoea and raised blood homocysteine accompany it. The most consequential fact about folate concerns pregnancy. The neural tube, which becomes the brain and spinal cord, closes around twenty eight days after conception, which is roughly the time a woman first misses a period. Adequate folate at that moment substantially reduces the risk of spina bifida and anencephaly, and by the time a pregnancy is confirmed the window has closed. The evidence is unusually strong: a British randomised trial reported in 1991 found that four milligrams a day cut recurrence of neural tube defects by about seventy per cent, and a Hungarian trial published in 1992 showed prevention of first occurrences. The resulting advice is that every woman who might become pregnant takes four hundred micrograms daily, with much higher doses for those who have had an affected pregnancy or take certain anticonvulsants. Because advice alone reaches only planned pregnancies, many countries fortify flour. The United States and Canada made it mandatory in January 1998, and neural tube defect rates fell by roughly a quarter to a third; more than eighty countries have followed, and the United Kingdom announced mandatory fortification of non wholemeal wheat flour in 2021. Synthetic folic acid is absorbed considerably better than natural food folate, which is why intakes are expressed as dietary folate equivalents that weight the two differently.

sections.heading: Vitamin B12: The Cobalt Vitamin and Its Elaborate Absorption
sections.body: Vitamin B12 is peculiar in almost every respect. It is the largest and most complex vitamin molecule, it is the only one containing a metal atom, cobalt, held at the centre of a ring structure related to the one in haemoglobin and chlorophyll, and it is made exclusively by bacteria and archaea. No plant, fungus or animal synthesises it. Animals obtain it from microbes, either from their own gut flora in species that can absorb it low in the digestive tract or from eating other animals, and this is why B12 is effectively confined to animal foods and why the question of supplementation is not optional for anyone avoiding them. It serves only two enzymes in the human body, but both are important. Methionine synthase, working in the cell fluid, uses a methyl bearing form of the vitamin to transfer a carbon from folate onto homocysteine, regenerating methionine. Methylmalonyl coenzyme A mutase, working inside mitochondria, uses a different form to rearrange a carbon skeleton in the breakdown of odd chain fatty acids and several amino acids. When the second enzyme fails, methylmalonic acid accumulates in blood and urine, which is why measuring it is the most specific available test of B12 status, considerably better than measuring the vitamin itself. The absorption pathway is the most elaborate of any nutrient. Stomach acid and pepsin release the vitamin from food protein. It binds a salivary protein for protection through the stomach, is released again in the duodenum by pancreatic enzymes, and then binds intrinsic factor, a glycoprotein secreted by the same stomach cells that make acid. Only the intrinsic factor complex is recognised by a specific receptor at the far end of the small intestine, where it is taken up and passed into the blood on a transport protein. Every step is a potential point of failure, which is why B12 deficiency is far more often a problem of absorption than of intake. The failures are worth naming. Autoimmune destruction of the acid producing stomach cells causes pernicious anaemia. Age related thinning of the stomach lining reduces acid and impairs release of vitamin bound to food, which is common enough that people over about fifty are advised to obtain B12 from fortified foods or supplements, where it is already free. Stomach or bariatric surgery, disease or removal of the terminal ileum, long term metformin, prolonged acid suppressing drugs, and certain intestinal parasites all interfere. Nitrous oxide, whether medical or recreational, irreversibly inactivates the cobalt atom and can precipitate severe deficiency within weeks. Deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia identical to that of folate lack, and separately a neurological disease in which the back and side columns of the spinal cord degenerate, producing loss of position sense, unsteadiness and eventually spastic weakness, along with peripheral neuropathy and cognitive change. Critically, the neurological damage can appear with no anaemia at all in around a quarter of cases, and unlike the anaemia it may not fully reverse.

sections.heading: The Methyl Trap: Why Folate and B12 Must Be Considered Together
sections.body: Folate and vitamin B12 meet at exactly one reaction, and that single junction explains why the two vitamins produce identical anaemias, why treating one can conceal a dangerous shortage of the other, and why a legal limit exists on how much folic acid may be added to food. The reaction is the remethylation of homocysteine to methionine, catalysed by methionine synthase. It requires B12 as the immediate carrier and takes its methyl group from a folate form called 5 methyltetrahydrofolate. The problem lies in an asymmetry upstream. The enzyme that produces 5 methyltetrahydrofolate runs effectively in one direction only, and methionine synthase is the sole route by which that form is converted back into the general purpose tetrahydrofolate needed for making DNA. If methionine synthase stalls for want of B12, folate flows into the methylated form and cannot get out. The cell may contain plenty of folate by any measurement and still be unable to use it. Researchers call this the methyl trap, and its consequence is that B12 deficiency creates a functional folate deficiency inside the cell, which is precisely why both vitamins produce the same enlarged, immature blood cells. The clinical danger follows directly. Give a large dose of folic acid to someone whose real problem is B12, and enough folate is forced through alternative routes to restore DNA synthesis. The anaemia improves, the blood count normalises, and the most visible warning sign disappears. Meanwhile the second B12 dependent enzyme, the mitochondrial mutase, remains blocked, and the degeneration of the spinal cord continues unopposed. People have been left permanently disabled this way, walking with a stick after their blood tests were pronounced normal. This is the entire reason the upper limit for folic acid from supplements and fortified food is set at one thousand micrograms a day, and the reason a clinician finding megaloblastic anaemia must establish B12 status before treating with folate rather than after. A related point concerns homocysteine. Deficiency of folate, B12 or B6 all raise blood homocysteine, and because raised homocysteine is associated with cardiovascular disease and dementia, it was widely assumed through the 1990s that supplementing these vitamins would prevent both. Large randomised trials published through the 2000s lowered homocysteine reliably and did not reduce heart attacks or deaths. Some analyses suggest a modest reduction in stroke, which remains debated. This is a genuinely instructive failure: a marker moved in the right direction without the disease following, and the honest position today is that homocysteine is a useful indicator of B vitamin status rather than a target worth treating in its own right. One further situation belongs here because it combines both hazards. Nitrous oxide inactivates the cobalt at the heart of vitamin B12 chemically and permanently, disabling methionine synthase and springing the methyl trap directly, without any dietary shortage at all. Heavy recreational use can produce spinal cord degeneration within weeks in a well nourished young person whose blood count and even whose serum B12 may look unremarkable, and it is now a regularly encountered cause of the condition in emergency departments.

sections.heading: Choline, the Vitamin-Like Compounds and the Missing Numbers
sections.body: Several substances sit near the B vitamins without quite belonging, and sorting out which are genuinely essential is the fastest way to see through a great deal of supplement marketing. Choline is the important one. It was formally recognised as an essential nutrient for humans only in 1998, and it is usually discussed alongside the B vitamins because its functions overlap with them directly. It is built into phosphatidylcholine, a principal component of every cell membrane, of the particles that export fat from the liver, and of the surfactant that keeps the lungs from collapsing. It is the raw material for acetylcholine, the neurotransmitter of the neuromuscular junction and much of the autonomic nervous system. And once oxidised to betaine it serves as an alternative methyl donor for converting homocysteine back to methionine, which is a direct backup for the folate and B12 pathway. Deficiency causes fat to accumulate in the liver and can damage muscle. Adequate intakes are set at about 550 milligrams a day for men and 425 for women, more in pregnancy and lactation, and surveys consistently show most people fall short. Eggs are the outstanding source, with a large egg supplying roughly 150 milligrams, followed by liver, meat and soy. The body makes some choline itself, by a pathway that depends on oestrogen, which means postmenopausal women rely more heavily on diet. Other compounds sold as B vitamins are not. Inositol, para aminobenzoic acid, carnitine and lipoic acid all have real biological roles, but healthy adults make enough of each, and none has an established deficiency disease from diet alone. Carnitine becomes conditionally essential in specific inherited disorders and in some people on dialysis, which is a medical situation rather than a dietary one, and inositol has been studied for particular conditions with results that remain preliminary. The gaps in the numbering are informative. Several were assigned to substances later shown not to be essential for humans: adenine took the number four, orotic acid thirteen. Two deserve to be named explicitly because they are still sold. Pangamic acid, marketed as B15, has never corresponded to any consistently defined chemical substance, and products bearing the name have contained different compounds in different decades. Amygdalin, marketed as B17 or laetrile, is not a vitamin by any definition, has no deficiency state and no established function in the body. It is a cyanogenic glycoside, meaning it releases hydrogen cyanide when broken down by gut bacteria. Clinical trials sponsored by the United States National Cancer Institute and reported in 1982 found no anticancer benefit and documented cyanide poisoning in participants, and deaths have occurred, particularly when the oral form was taken alongside foods containing enzymes that accelerate cyanide release. Anything described as vitamin B15 or B17 should be treated as a marketing label rather than a nutrient.

sections.heading: Deficiency: How It Presents and Who Is Actually at Risk
sections.body: Because the B vitamins become coenzymes serving overlapping pathways, their deficiencies produce overlapping symptoms, and no honest account can pretend that a person can identify which vitamin they are short of from how they feel. Four systems dominate the picture in nearly every case. The lining of the mouth and tongue becomes sore, smooth and inflamed, and the corners of the mouth crack. The skin develops scaling and redness, typically around the nose, eyebrows and behind the ears. The blood shows anaemia, though of different kinds: enlarged immature cells with folate and B12, small pale cells with B6, ordinary sized cells with riboflavin. And the nervous system produces some combination of numbness, burning or tingling in the feet and hands, unsteadiness, low mood, irritability and confusion. Add fatigue, which accompanies all of them and a thousand other things, and it becomes obvious why testing rather than guessing is the only sound approach. The risk groups, by contrast, are well defined and are what should prompt investigation. Chronic heavy alcohol use is the largest, impairing intake, absorption and activation of thiamin in particular, and folate, B6 and riboflavin alongside it. Older adults commonly develop thinning of the stomach lining that impairs release of vitamin B12 from food, which is why guidance in several countries advises people over about fifty to take B12 in the free crystalline form found in fortified foods and supplements. People eating no animal foods will eventually become B12 deficient without supplementation; this is not a matter of opinion, and the consequences in a breastfed infant of a deficient mother can be severe and incompletely reversible. Surgery and disease of the digestive tract matter enormously. Bariatric surgery requires lifelong supplementation, particularly of thiamin, B12 and folate. Coeliac disease, Crohn's disease, pancreatic insufficiency and resection of the last part of the small intestine all impair absorption. Dialysis removes water soluble vitamins directly. Pregnancy and lactation raise requirements across the board, and severe pregnancy vomiting has caused Wernicke encephalopathy. Medicines are the most easily overlooked cause. Metformin and long term acid suppressing drugs reduce B12 absorption. Isoniazid, cycloserine, penicillamine and hydralazine deplete B6. Methotrexate, trimethoprim, sulfasalazine and phenytoin interfere with folate. Older anticonvulsants affect biotin. Loop diuretics increase thiamin losses. In any unexplained case, reviewing the medication list is frequently more productive than reviewing the diet. Testing is imperfect and worth understanding before requesting it. Serum B12 has a wide ambiguous band in which the result neither confirms nor excludes deficiency, and methylmalonic acid, which rises specifically when the B12 dependent mitochondrial enzyme is blocked, resolves most of those cases. Serum folate reflects recent meals and can look normal in someone chronically depleted, so red cell folate is the better measure of stores. Thiamin status is assessed by measuring the coenzyme in whole blood or by the responsiveness of a red cell enzyme to added thiamin, and riboflavin and B6 have their own functional tests. Because results take days and the consequences of delay are neurological, clinicians facing a convincing clinical picture routinely start treatment first and let the laboratory confirm afterwards, which is the correct order of operations.

sections.heading: Food Sources and How Cooking Destroys or Preserves Them
sections.body: Because these vitamins dissolve in water, the dominant loss in cooking is not destruction but escape into the pan. Boiling vegetables and pouring the water away can remove thirty to fifty per cent of the folate and thiamin present, intact but elsewhere. Steaming, brief microwaving, or keeping the liquid for a sauce recovers most of it. Heat sensitivity varies sharply. Thiamin is the most fragile: degraded by prolonged heat, destroyed rapidly in alkaline conditions, which is why adding bicarbonate of soda to green vegetables is a bad habit, and broken down by sulphite preservatives and by enzymes in raw freshwater fish. Folate is sensitive to heat and oxygen, losing half or more in long boiling. Riboflavin shrugs off heat but is destroyed by light. Niacin, B6, biotin and pantothenic acid are comparatively robust. Milling matters more than cooking. Polishing brown rice to white removes roughly four fifths of its thiamin along with the bran and germ, which is exactly how beriberi became epidemic. Maize runs the other way: its niacin is bound in a form the gut cannot use, and soaking the grain in wood ash or slaked lime before grinding releases it.
ingredients: Liver from beef, lamb or chicken: the richest single source by a wide margin, supplying B12, folate, riboflavin, niacin, B6, biotin and pantothenic acid together; one small portion a fortnight covers a great deal.
Whole grains, oats and wheat germ: thiamin, niacin, B6 and pantothenic acid, concentrated in the bran and germ that refining removes; wheat germ can be bought separately and stirred into anything.
Legumes, especially lentils, chickpeas and black beans: among the best plant sources of folate and thiamin, plus useful B6; dried and cheap, and canned versions retain most of it.
Dark leafy greens such as spinach and kale: the original source from which folate was isolated and named; best lightly cooked or raw, since prolonged boiling destroys much of it.

Eggs: biotin, B12, riboflavin and pantothenic acid, plus the best everyday source of choline at roughly 150 milligrams in one large egg; cook the white, which denatures the biotin binding protein avidin.
Milk, yoghurt and cheese: the main riboflavin source in many diets, plus B12; buy milk in opaque containers, since sunlight through clear glass destroys much of the riboflavin within hours.
Meat, poultry and oily fish: B12, niacin, B6 and pantothenic acid; salmon and tuna are particularly good for B6 and B12 at once.
Clams, mussels and other shellfish: extraordinarily concentrated in B12, often several times a day's requirement in one modest serving.

Nutritional yeast and yeast extract spreads: rich in most B vitamins, and versions explicitly fortified with B12 are a reliable non animal source; check the label, since unfortified yeast contains none.
Fortified breakfast cereals and plant milks: often the most practical source of B12 and folic acid for people avoiding animal foods; amounts are printed on the packet and vary widely.
Sunflower seeds, peanuts and pistachios: thiamin, niacin, B6 and pantothenic acid, useful because they need no cooking.
Potatoes, bananas and avocados: everyday contributors of vitamin B6; baking potatoes in their skins retains far more than boiling them peeled.

sections.heading: Fortification, Supplements and Upper Limits
sections.body: Public health fortification has been one of the most successful interventions in the history of nutrition, and it works precisely because it reaches people who are not thinking about their diet at all. The United States began enriching white flour with thiamin, riboflavin, niacin and iron in 1941, and pellagra and beriberi, which had been endemic, effectively disappeared from industrialised countries within a generation. Folic acid was added to the same enrichment standard from January 1998 in the United States and Canada, and rates of spina bifida and anencephaly fell by roughly a quarter to a third almost immediately. More than eighty countries now fortify flour with folic acid. Supplements have a narrower and more specific role. The groups who genuinely benefit are identifiable rather than universal: any woman who might become pregnant should take four hundred micrograms of folic acid daily, beginning before conception rather than after a positive test; anyone eating no animal foods needs a reliable B12 source; adults over about fifty should obtain B12 from fortified food or a supplement because they may no longer release it from food protein; people after bariatric surgery need lifelong supplementation; people with pernicious anaemia need either injections or high dose oral B12; people using isoniazid need pyridoxine; and people with heavy alcohol use need thiamin. For most other adults eating a varied diet, a supplement changes nothing measurable. One mechanism is worth understanding because it saves a lot of injections. The elaborate intrinsic factor pathway that normally absorbs B12 saturates at roughly one to two micrograms per meal, but a completely separate passive route absorbs about one per cent of whatever is present in the gut regardless of intrinsic factor. A daily dose of one to two thousand micrograms therefore delivers ten to twenty micrograms by simple diffusion, which is why high dose oral B12 works even in people who have no intrinsic factor at all. Upper limits exist for exactly three of the eight, and each has a specific reason. Niacin is capped at thirty five milligrams a day from supplements and fortified food because of flushing and, at higher doses, liver injury. Vitamin B6 is capped at one hundred milligrams a day because of nerve damage. Folic acid is capped at one thousand micrograms a day because it masks B12 deficiency. Thiamin, riboflavin, pantothenic acid, biotin and B12 have no established upper limit. Crucially, these limits apply to synthetic and fortified forms, not to the vitamins as they occur naturally in food. Two marketing claims deserve scepticism. Products offering methylcobalamin instead of the cheaper cyanocobalamin are sold as more natural and better absorbed, and there is no convincing evidence that this matters for ordinary supplementation. Products offering methylfolate on the grounds of a common variant in the gene for one folate enzyme are similar: the variant is real and reduces the enzyme's activity, but professional genetics bodies do not recommend routine testing for it, and ordinary folic acid works perfectly well for the great majority of people who carry it.

sections.heading: Excess, Uncertainty and What to Do When Something Is Wrong
sections.body: The popular belief that water soluble vitamins are harmless because the excess is simply excreted is mostly true and dangerously incomplete. Four exceptions account for essentially all the documented harm. Vitamin B6 taken at high doses over months causes a sensory nerve damage that can be slow to reverse and occasionally does not. Nicotinic acid at gram doses causes flushing, can injure the liver, and raises blood glucose and uric acid. Folic acid conceals the blood signs of B12 deficiency while nerve damage proceeds. And high dose biotin distorts a wide range of laboratory tests, in one direction or the other depending on the assay, with a documented death from a missed heart attack. Everything else is largely harmless in excess, which is why the sensible position is neither fear nor enthusiasm but specificity. A parallel set of claims has no support at all. B vitamins do not supply energy; they permit the release of energy from food, so taking more when you already have enough produces nothing but expensive urine. Injections of B12 for tiredness in people with normal levels have been given for decades on no evidence. High dose biotin for hair and nails rests on case reports in people who were genuinely deficient. And the substances marketed as vitamins B15 and B17 are not vitamins, the latter being a cyanide releasing compound with documented poisonings. Several things remain genuinely unsettled, and it is more useful to say so than to project confidence. Recommended intakes were derived to prevent deficiency, and whether higher intakes benefit anyone who is already replete is largely unproven. The long term significance of unmetabolised folic acid circulating in people with high intakes is not established. The relationship between folate and cancer risk appears to run in different directions at different stages of disease and is not resolved. The blood concentration of B12 below which harm occurs is genuinely blurred, with a wide grey zone in which methylmalonic acid measurement is more informative than the vitamin level itself. And the newer compounds marketed as NAD precursors have interesting biology and thin human evidence. When something seems wrong, the practical sequence is straightforward. Do not attempt to identify a specific deficiency from symptoms, because they overlap almost completely; ask for testing instead. Take neurological symptoms seriously and promptly, since numbness, unsteadiness or memory change from B12 deficiency can become permanent while blood counts still look acceptable. Never treat a large cell anaemia with folate until B12 has been checked. If you are at risk of thiamin depletion through alcohol, starvation or severe vomiting and become unwell, thiamin must be given before or with any glucose. Stop biotin supplements at least three days before blood tests and mention them. Review your medication list, which is a more common cause than diet in wealthy countries. Fix the diet where the problem is intake and supplement where the problem is absorption. And always retest after treatment, because a deficiency that fails to respond was probably never the diagnosis.

guides.safetyNote: This is general education, not medical advice. Four points carry real risk. Do not treat a large-cell anaemia with folic acid until vitamin B12 has been measured, because folate can correct the blood picture while B12-related spinal cord damage continues and becomes permanent. Anyone at risk of thiamin depletion through heavy alcohol use, starvation, severe pregnancy vomiting or refeeding must receive thiamin before or alongside intravenous glucose. Do not exceed 100 mg a day of vitamin B6 long term, as sustained higher intakes cause nerve damage that may not fully reverse. And stop high-dose biotin supplements at least three days before any blood test and tell the clinician, as biotin distorts many common assays including thyroid and heart-attack tests. Numbness, unsteadiness or memory change should be assessed by a clinician promptly rather than self-treated.

guides.title: Minerals: Iron, Calcium, Zinc and Magnesium
guides.summary: A full account of the four minerals most often deficient in human diets: what each one does in the body, how absorption is regulated, which foods supply them, how deficiency and excess present, and how supplementation is done safely.

sections.heading: Why Minerals Matter and What Makes Them Different from Vitamins
sections.body:
Minerals are chemical elements the body cannot make and cannot destroy. Unlike vitamins, which are organic molecules built from carbon skeletons and can be synthesised by plants, microbes or in a laboratory, a mineral is an atom of a particular element that must ultimately be mined out of rock, taken up by plant roots, and passed along a food chain into your tissues. Every iron atom in your blood was forged in a star, weathered out of soil, absorbed by a plant, and eaten. There is no other route.

This has a practical consequence that runs through everything that follows. Because minerals are elements, the body's only options are to absorb them, store them, use them, or excrete them. It cannot break down an excess iron atom the way it can metabolise excess vitamin C. Regulation therefore happens almost entirely at the gate, in the intestine, and to a lesser extent at the kidney. That is why mineral nutrition is dominated by questions of bioavailability, meaning how much of what you swallow actually crosses the gut wall, rather than by how much is on the label.

Nutritionists divide minerals into macrominerals, needed in amounts above about 100 milligrams a day, and trace minerals, needed in milligram or microgram quantities. Calcium and magnesium are macrominerals; iron and zinc are trace minerals, though iron sits near the boundary. The four covered here are grouped together because they are, by a wide margin, the minerals most commonly deficient worldwide, and because their absorption is interlinked in ways that make them impossible to understand in isolation. Calcium blocks iron uptake. Zinc and iron compete for the same transporter. Magnesium is required for the enzyme that activates vitamin D, which in turn controls calcium absorption. Change one and you change the others.

The scale of the problem is enormous. The World Health Organization estimates that around two billion people are affected by micronutrient deficiencies, with iron deficiency alone affecting roughly a quarter of the world's population and causing about half of all anaemia. Zinc deficiency is estimated to contribute to hundreds of thousands of childhood deaths a year through diarrhoeal disease and pneumonia. Calcium intake is below recommended levels across most of Asia and Africa. Magnesium intake falls short of the recommended amount for roughly half the population of the United States and much of Europe.

Yet none of these are exotic conditions. They arise from ordinary diets built on refined grains, low in animal foods, high in phytate-rich unfermented staples, or simply low in total variety. Understanding what each mineral does, what blocks it, and what the honest evidence says about supplementing it is one of the highest-return pieces of practical knowledge in nutrition, and it is knowledge that has changed substantially in the last two decades.

sections.heading: Bioavailability: Why the Number on the Label Is Not the Number You Absorb
sections.body:
The single most important idea in mineral nutrition is that intake and absorption are different quantities, often by a factor of five or more. A cup of spinach contains a respectable amount of calcium and iron on paper; almost none of it reaches your bloodstream, because both are locked up by oxalate. Understanding what governs that gap explains most of the practical advice in this field.

Absorption of minerals happens mainly in the small intestine, and the mineral must be in a soluble, usually ionised, form to be taken up by a transporter protein. Anything that binds the mineral into an insoluble complex before it reaches the absorptive surface removes it from play. The three great binders are phytate, oxalate and, to a lesser extent, some polyphenols.

Phytic acid, or inositol hexaphosphate, is the storage form of phosphorus in seeds. It is abundant in whole grains, legumes, nuts and seeds, and it carries six negatively charged phosphate groups that chelate positively charged mineral ions with high affinity. It binds zinc most strongly, then iron, then calcium and magnesium. A phytate-to-zinc molar ratio above about 15 predicts poor zinc status at a population level, and ratios above 20 are common in diets based on unleavened wholemeal bread or unfermented maize. This is why zinc deficiency was first characterised in the 1960s by Ananda Prasad among adolescents in rural Iran and Egypt whose diets were dominated by unleavened wholewheat flatbread.

Oxalate is a small dicarboxylic acid concentrated in spinach, rhubarb, beet greens, chard, sorrel and to a lesser degree in tea and nuts. It forms almost completely insoluble calcium oxalate. Calcium absorption from spinach is roughly 5 percent, against about 32 percent from milk and above 50 percent from low-oxalate brassicas like kale, broccoli and bok choy. Spinach's reputation as an iron food comes from a mixture of high measured iron content and low actual availability.

Polyphenols and tannins in tea, coffee, cocoa and red wine bind non-haem iron strongly. A cup of tea taken with a meal can cut iron absorption from that meal by 60 percent or more; coffee by around 40 percent.

Working the other way, several enhancers exist. Ascorbic acid, vitamin C, is the most powerful: it reduces ferric iron to the absorbable ferrous form and keeps it soluble, and 50 milligrams, roughly the amount in half an orange, can double or triple non-haem iron uptake from a meal. Animal tissue contains a poorly-characterised "meat factor" that improves both iron and zinc uptake. Fermentation, soaking, sprouting and sourdough leavening all activate the enzyme phytase, which degrades phytate; long-fermented sourdough can remove most of the phytate from wholemeal bread, which is why traditional bread-making methods were quietly solving a nutritional problem their inventors could not have described.

sections.heading: Iron: What It Does and Where It Sits in the Body
sections.body:
An adult body contains roughly three to four grams of iron, about the mass of a small nail, and almost all of it is doing one of two jobs: carrying oxygen, or transferring electrons.

Around 60 to 70 percent of body iron sits in haemoglobin, the protein filling every red blood cell. Haemoglobin is a tetramer of four globin chains, each cradling a haem group, and each haem group holds a single ferrous iron atom in the centre of a flat porphyrin ring. That iron atom binds one molecule of oxygen reversibly. Four haems means four oxygen molecules per haemoglobin, and roughly 270 million haemoglobin molecules per red cell, which is how a teaspoon of blood carries enough oxygen to matter. The binding is cooperative: as each oxygen binds, the protein shifts shape and the remaining sites bind more readily, producing the characteristic sigmoid oxygen dissociation curve that lets haemoglobin load fully in the lungs and unload steeply in working tissue.

Another 10 percent or so sits in myoglobin, the single-chain relative of haemoglobin that stores oxygen inside muscle, and gives red meat its colour. A further few percent occupies the iron-sulphur clusters and cytochromes of the mitochondrial electron transport chain, where iron cycles between the ferrous and ferric states to shuttle electrons down the chain that ultimately produces ATP. Iron is also required by ribonucleotide reductase, the enzyme that makes DNA precursors, by several enzymes of neurotransmitter synthesis including tyrosine hydroxylase, and by the myelin-producing oligodendrocytes of the brain.

The remainder, typically 20 to 25 percent in a healthy adult, is stored, mostly as ferritin. Ferritin is a hollow protein shell of 24 subunits that can sequester up to about 4,500 iron atoms as a ferric oxyhydroxide mineral core, keeping them soluble and chemically inert. Haemosiderin is a denser, partly degraded form of the same store found in iron overload. Serum ferritin, which leaks from cells in proportion to stores, is the standard clinical measure of body iron, though it also rises with inflammation, which makes interpretation harder than it looks.

The reason iron must be so carefully bound at all times is that free iron is dangerous. Ferrous iron reacts with hydrogen peroxide in the Fenton reaction to produce the hydroxyl radical, one of the most destructive oxidants in biology, which attacks lipids, proteins and DNA indiscriminately. The body therefore keeps essentially no free iron: it is bound to transferrin in the blood, to ferritin in storage, and inserted directly into proteins at the point of use. This dual character, indispensable and toxic, explains why iron regulation is unusually elaborate and why iron supplementation should never be casual.

sections.heading: How the Body Controls Iron: Hepcidin and the One-Way Door
sections.body:
Human beings have no regulated mechanism for excreting iron. There is no iron equivalent of urinating out excess sodium. Losses are passive and small: roughly one milligram a day in men and postmenopausal women, shed in sloughed intestinal cells, skin cells and small amounts of blood. Menstruating women lose an additional average of about 0.5 milligrams a day, though with wide variation, and a single pregnancy costs something like 500 to 1,000 milligrams net.

Because the exit is fixed, everything must be regulated at the entrance, and the system that does it was only properly understood after 2000, with the discovery of the hormone hepcidin by Tomas Ganz, Elizabeta Nemeth and others. Hepcidin is a small 25-amino-acid peptide made by the liver. Its target is ferroportin, the only known protein that exports iron out of a cell into the blood. Ferroportin sits on the basolateral membrane of intestinal absorptive cells, on macrophages that recycle iron from old red cells, and on liver storage cells. When hepcidin binds ferroportin, the transporter is internalised and destroyed. Iron stops leaving cells, so dietary iron taken into the gut lining never reaches the blood and is simply lost when that cell is shed a few days later.

Hepcidin production rises when iron stores are full, and it rises sharply during inflammation, driven by the cytokine interleukin-6. This second response is an ancient defence: many bacteria need iron to multiply, so hiding iron inside cells starves them. The cost is that any chronic inflammatory state, from rheumatoid arthritis to chronic kidney disease to persistent infection, produces the anaemia of chronic disease, in which the body has adequate iron but cannot mobilise it. Giving oral iron in that state does very little, because hepcidin is blocking the door.

On the absorptive side, dietary non-haem iron in the ferric state is first reduced to ferrous by the brush-border enzyme duodenal cytochrome b, then carried across the apical membrane by divalent metal transporter 1, or DMT1. DMT1 is not selective: it also transports zinc, copper, manganese, cobalt and, unhelpfully, lead and cadmium. This lack of selectivity is why iron deficiency increases lead absorption, and why iron-deficient children in areas with lead exposure are at compounded risk: the transporter is upregulated to scavenge iron and admits lead along with it.

Haem iron takes a separate and better-understood-by-outcome-than-by-mechanism route, entering the enterocyte intact and having its iron released internally by haem oxygenase. Because it bypasses the phytate and polyphenol problem entirely, haem iron is absorbed at roughly 15 to 35 percent regardless of what else is in the meal, against 2 to 20 percent for non-haem iron depending heavily on meal composition and body stores.

sections.heading: Iron Deficiency: Recognising It, Measuring It, Correcting It
sections.body:
Iron deficiency develops in stages, and the familiar anaemia is the last of them. First, stores deplete: serum ferritin falls while haemoglobin stays normal and the person may already feel tired. Second, iron-deficient erythropoiesis begins: transferrin saturation falls below about 16 percent, soluble transferrin receptor rises, and red cell production becomes constrained. Only third does haemoglobin drop below the diagnostic threshold, conventionally 130 grams per litre in men and 120 in non-pregnant women, producing microcytic hypochromic anaemia in which red cells are small, with a mean corpuscular volume below about 80 femtolitres, and pale.

Symptoms progress accordingly: fatigue, reduced exercise tolerance, breathlessness on exertion, poor concentration, cold intolerance, hair shedding, brittle spoon-shaped nails known as koilonychia, cracks at the corners of the mouth, and restless legs syndrome, which responds to iron in a substantial minority of cases. Pica, the compulsive eating of non-foods, most characteristically ice, is a curious and quite specific sign. In children, iron deficiency in the first two years is associated with lasting deficits in cognitive and motor development that may not fully reverse with later treatment, which is why infant iron status is treated as urgent.

Diagnosis rests on ferritin as the first-line test. Below 15 micrograms per litre is diagnostic of depleted stores; below 30 is widely treated as deficient in symptomatic patients. The complication is that ferritin is an acute-phase protein and rises with any inflammation, so a normal ferritin does not exclude deficiency if C-reactive protein is raised. In that situation transferrin saturation, soluble transferrin receptor, or a therapeutic trial is used instead.

Crucially, iron deficiency in an adult, particularly a man or a postmenopausal woman, is a symptom and not a diagnosis. The commonest causes are menstrual loss, pregnancy, and inadequate intake, but occult gastrointestinal bleeding from ulcers, coeliac disease or colorectal cancer must be excluded. Treating the anaemia without asking why it happened has cost lives.

Treatment with oral iron is effective but poorly tolerated. Typical adult doses are 100 to 200 milligrams of elemental iron daily as ferrous sulphate, fumarate or gluconate. Important nuance from the last decade: a single dose raises hepcidin for up to 24 hours, so alternate-day dosing of a single tablet actually achieves greater total absorption than divided daily dosing, with fewer side effects. Take it on an empty stomach with vitamin C if tolerated; avoid tea, coffee, calcium supplements and antacids within two hours. Expect black stools, which are harmless, and constipation or nausea in perhaps a third of people. Haemoglobin should rise by about 10 grams per litre within two to four weeks; continue for three months after normalisation to refill stores. Intravenous iron is now safe and routine where oral iron fails or is not absorbed.

sections.heading: Iron Sources, Excess and the Genetics of Overload
sections.body:
Dietary iron divides sharply into haem and non-haem forms, and the distinction matters more than the raw milligram figures. Haem iron comes only from animal flesh and blood, and typically makes up 40 percent or so of the iron in meat. Liver is exceptionally rich, at roughly 6 to 18 milligrams per 100 grams depending on species, followed by red meat at 2 to 3 milligrams, and poultry and fish at around 1. Blood-based foods such as black pudding are among the densest iron foods known. Shellfish, especially clams, oysters and mussels, are outstanding, with clams reaching 20 milligrams or more per 100 grams.

Non-haem iron is more widely distributed but much less available: lentils and beans at 2 to 3 milligrams per 100 grams cooked, tofu, pumpkin and sesame seeds, cashews, dark chocolate, and fortified breakfast cereals which are often the single largest contributor in Western diets. Fortification of flour with iron is mandatory in more than 80 countries and has measurably reduced anaemia where implemented well. Cooking acidic foods in cast iron genuinely transfers useful amounts of iron, and the Lucky Iron Fish, a cast-iron ingot added to cooking pots, was developed on that principle for use in Cambodia with mixed but generally positive trial results.

Requirements vary widely. Adult men and postmenopausal women need about 8 milligrams a day; menstruating women about 18; pregnancy raises the figure to about 27. Vegetarians and vegans are conventionally advised to aim for roughly 1.8 times these figures because of the lower availability of non-haem iron, though adaptation over time partly offsets this.

Excess iron is a real hazard and moves in the opposite direction from most nutritional advice. Acute iron poisoning from swallowed supplements is the leading cause of fatal poisoning in children under six; doses above 20 milligrams of elemental iron per kilogram of body weight cause vomiting and gastrointestinal corrosion, and above 60 milligrams per kilogram can be lethal through shock and liver failure. Iron tablets must be stored like medicines, not like vitamins.

Chronic overload is usually genetic. Hereditary haemochromatosis, most often caused by homozygous C282Y mutation in the HFE gene, impairs hepcidin production so absorption stays high regardless of stores. It is among the commonest genetic disorders in people of northern European ancestry, with roughly 1 in 200 homozygous, though penetrance is incomplete and many never develop disease. Untreated, iron accumulates over decades in liver, pancreas, heart, joints and pituitary, producing cirrhosis, diabetes, cardiomyopathy, arthritis and hypogonadism. The old name "bronze diabetes" captured the skin pigmentation and glucose intolerance. Treatment is elegantly simple: repeated venesection, removing 450 to 500 millilitres of blood, each unit taking about 250 milligrams of iron with it.

sections.heading: Calcium: The Skeleton as a Bank Account
sections.body:
Calcium is the most abundant mineral in the body by a wide margin. An adult carries roughly 1,000 to 1,200 grams, more than a kilogram, and about 99 percent of it is in bone and teeth as hydroxyapatite, a crystalline calcium phosphate with the approximate formula Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2. That mineral phase, deposited on a scaffold of type I collagen, is what gives bone its compressive strength; the collagen provides tensile strength and toughness. Bone is a composite material in the engineering sense, and like any composite it fails when either phase is compromised.

The remaining one percent, roughly 10 grams, is in blood, extracellular fluid and inside cells, and it is this tiny fraction that the body defends with absolute priority. Blood ionised calcium is held between about 1.1 and 1.3 millimoles per litre, a range narrower than almost any other physiological variable, because calcium is the universal intracellular signal. A calcium influx triggers the contraction of every muscle fibre by binding troponin C and freeing the actin binding site; it triggers neurotransmitter release at every synapse; it activates the clotting cascade, where it is coagulation factor IV; and it acts as a second messenger for hundreds of hormones through calmodulin.

Because the signal must be sharp, resting cytosolic calcium is kept extraordinarily low, around 100 nanomolar, roughly ten thousand times lower than outside the cell. That gradient is maintained by ATP-driven pumps in the plasma membrane and the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Contraction is not the cell spending energy to pull; it is the cell spending energy continuously to keep calcium out, then briefly letting it in.

The consequence of this priority system is the central fact of calcium nutrition: the skeleton is a reservoir, and the body will demineralise it without hesitation to keep blood calcium correct. Low dietary calcium does not cause low blood calcium in a healthy person. It causes bone loss, silently, over years. You cannot detect calcium deficiency from a routine blood test, which is a persistent source of false reassurance.

Bone itself is not inert. It is continuously remodelled by two cell types working in coupled units: osteoclasts, large multinucleate cells that dissolve mineral by secreting acid and digest collagen with cathepsin K, and osteoblasts, which lay down new collagen matrix and mineralise it. The entire adult skeleton is replaced roughly every ten years, with trabecular bone in the spine turning over several times faster than cortical bone in the shafts of long bones. Peak bone mass is reached somewhere between the late teens and about age 30, and everything after that is a slow net loss, accelerating sharply in women for five to ten years after menopause as oestrogen withdrawal removes a brake on osteoclast activity.

sections.heading: Calcium Regulation: Parathyroid Hormone, Vitamin D and Calcitonin
sections.body:
Blood calcium is controlled by a three-hormone system that acts on three organs: gut, bone and kidney. Understanding it explains why vitamin D matters so much and why calcium supplements behave the way they do.

The sensor is the calcium-sensing receptor on the surface of the parathyroid glands, four rice-grain-sized glands behind the thyroid. When ionised calcium falls even slightly, the receptor releases its inhibition and the glands secrete parathyroid hormone, PTH, an 84-amino-acid peptide. PTH does three things. In bone, it stimulates osteoblasts to produce RANK ligand, which activates osteoclasts to resorb bone and release calcium and phosphate. In the kidney, it increases calcium reabsorption in the distal tubule while promoting phosphate excretion. And, most importantly for nutrition, it activates the enzyme 1-alpha-hydroxylase in the kidney, which converts the storage form of vitamin D, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, into the active hormone 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, also called calcitriol.

Calcitriol is the agent that actually raises calcium absorption from food. It enters intestinal cells, binds the vitamin D receptor, and switches on transcription of the calcium channel TRPV6, the intracellular carrier calbindin, and the basolateral calcium pump. Without adequate vitamin D, active calcium absorption collapses to perhaps 10 to 15 percent of intake, against 30 to 40 percent when vitamin D status is good. This is why calcium and vitamin D are almost always discussed together, and why severe vitamin D deficiency produces rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults: bone matrix is laid down but cannot be mineralised, so the skeleton becomes soft rather than merely thin.

Calcitonin, secreted by the thyroid's parafollicular C cells when calcium is high, opposes PTH by inhibiting osteoclasts. In humans its physiological role is modest; people without a thyroid do not develop calcium disorders. It matters more as a pharmacological tool and in other species.

Two nutritional implications follow. First, chronically low calcium intake produces chronically elevated PTH, called secondary hyperparathyroidism, which is a slow bone-resorbing state. It is common in older adults with poor sun exposure and low dairy intake, and correcting vitamin D alone will not fix it if calcium intake is genuinely inadequate.

Second, absorption is dose-dependent and saturable. Fractional absorption falls as the single dose rises: about 36 percent from a 300 milligram load, but only around 28 percent from 1,000 milligrams. This is the reason supplements should be split into doses of 500 milligrams or less taken at separate times. Calcium carbonate, the cheapest and densest form at 40 percent elemental calcium, requires stomach acid and must be taken with food; calcium citrate, at 21 percent elemental, is absorbed regardless of acid and suits people on proton pump inhibitors or with achlorhydria.

sections.heading: Calcium Sources, Requirements and the Supplement Controversy
sections.body:
Adult requirements are set at roughly 1,000 milligrams a day for most adults, rising to 1,200 for women over 50 and everyone over 70, with adolescents needing about 1,300 during the years of fastest skeletal accrual. These are the figures used in the United States; the United Kingdom sets a notably lower reference nutrient intake of 700 milligrams for adults, and the WHO uses 1,000 to 1,300 depending on group. The disagreement is genuine and reflects real uncertainty about how much is optimal rather than merely adequate.

Dairy is the densest common source: 240 millilitres of milk provides about 300 milligrams, a similar amount of yoghurt slightly more, and 30 grams of hard cheese around 200. Absorption from dairy is around 32 percent. Canned fish eaten with the bones, sardines and salmon in particular, are excellent, at 300 to 400 milligrams per 100 grams. Among plants, the key distinction is oxalate content. Low-oxalate brassicas such as kale, broccoli, bok choy, collards and Chinese cabbage give absorption of 50 to 60 percent, the highest of any food, though the total per serving is modest. Spinach, chard and beet greens, despite high calcium content, deliver almost nothing. Calcium-set tofu, made with calcium sulphate, provides 200 to 350 milligrams per 100 grams; almonds, tahini, figs and fortified plant milks all contribute. Hard tap water in limestone regions can supply 100 milligrams a litre or more, a genuinely significant and usually ignored source.

The supplement question has become one of the more contested areas in nutrition. Trials consistently show that calcium plus vitamin D modestly reduces fracture risk in institutionalised and vitamin-D-deficient older people, with a number needed to treat in the low hundreds. Evidence for benefit in healthy, community-dwelling, replete adults is much weaker, and several large analyses have found essentially none. Meanwhile, a series of analyses since 2010, notably by Mark Bolland and colleagues, reported a small increase in myocardial infarction with calcium supplements taken without vitamin D, on the order of a 20 to 30 percent relative increase. The finding remains disputed; other groups and the National Osteoporosis Foundation have not found the association, and mechanisms proposed, such as a transient post-dose rise in serum calcium promoting vascular calcification, are plausible but unproven.

The defensible position given the current evidence is this: aim to meet calcium needs from food, where no cardiovascular signal has ever been seen and where the mineral arrives slowly with protein, phosphorus and other nutrients. Reserve supplements for people who genuinely cannot reach adequate intake from diet, keep supplemental doses modest, at 500 milligrams or less at a time, and pair them with adequate vitamin D. Do not exceed a total intake, food plus supplements, of about 2,000 to 2,500 milligrams a day, above which kidney stone risk rises measurably.

sections.heading: Zinc: The Structural Element of the Proteome
sections.body:
Zinc is present in the body in only about two to three grams, comparable to iron, but it is functionally far more widespread. Well over 300 enzymes require zinc, and current structural estimates suggest that around 10 percent of all human proteins, some 3,000 of them, bind zinc. It is the second most abundant trace metal in the body and the only one found in all six enzyme classes.

Zinc plays three distinguishable roles. Catalytically, it sits in enzyme active sites where its stable divalent charge and lack of redox activity make it ideal for polarising water molecules and stabilising negative transition states. Carbonic anhydrase, which interconverts carbon dioxide and bicarbonate at a rate approaching a million reactions per second and underlies both respiration and stomach acid secretion, is a zinc enzyme. So are alcohol dehydrogenase, carboxypeptidase, alkaline phosphatase, and the matrix metalloproteinases that remodel connective tissue.

Structurally, zinc holds proteins in shape.
