Reintroducing carbohydrate to a severely malnourished person triggers a surge of insulin that drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium out of the blood and into cells; the resulting plasma collapse causes cardiac arrhythmia, respiratory failure and death, sometimes within seventy-two hours. This is refeeding syndrome, and it kills people who have just been rescued. Refeeding must be slow — starting near 10 kcal per kilogram per day and increasing over days — with thiamin given before any carbohydrate and with electrolytes monitored, ideally under medical supervision.

Everything here is educational. Nutrition interacts with prescribed medication, pregnancy, and kidney and liver disease in ways that change the numbers substantially. Seek qualified medical or dietetic care for diagnosis and treatment, and do not attempt to self-treat a suspected deficiency that is already producing symptoms.

sections.heading: Cellular Respiration: How Macronutrients Actually Become ATP
sections.body:
Digestion and absorption only get fuel to the doorstep of the cell; the actual "use" promised in this guide's title happens in the cytoplasm and mitochondria, and it is worth tracing all the way through because the numbers explain why fat is such a dense fuel and why the brain is so picky about glucose.

Glucose's first stop is glycolysis, a ten-enzyme sequence in the cytosol that splits one 6-carbon glucose into two 3-carbon pyruvate molecules. It costs 2 ATP to prime the molecule (hexokinase and phosphofructokinase both consume ATP) and repays 4 ATP plus 2 NADH downstream, for a net yield of 2 ATP and 2 NADH per glucose — and it runs with or without oxygen, which is why anaerobic muscle can still make some ATP during an all-out sprint. If oxygen is available, pyruvate is ferried into the mitochondrial matrix and decarboxylated by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex into acetyl-CoA (releasing 1 CO2 and generating 1 NADH per pyruvate — 2 per glucose). Acetyl-CoA then enters the citric acid cycle, a closed loop of eight reactions that, per turn, releases 2 CO2 and generates 3 NADH, 1 FADH2 and 1 GTP (readily swapped for ATP) — and because each glucose yields two acetyl-CoA, the cycle turns twice per glucose.

The real payoff comes at the electron transport chain, where NADH and FADH2 hand electrons down protein complexes embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane, pumping protons out to build an electrochemical gradient that ATP synthase spins like a turbine to phosphorylate ADP. Using modern accounting (roughly 2.5 ATP per NADH, 1.5 ATP per FADH2 — lower than the classic 3:2 textbook figures because some of the gradient leaks and some is spent shuttling NADH's electrons across the mitochondrial membrane), one glucose nets out to about 30–32 ATP total. Fat tells a different story: a 16-carbon palmitate molecule is chopped into 8 acetyl-CoA units by beta-oxidation, a cycle that itself throws off 1 FADH2 and 1 NADH per cut, and by the time all 8 acetyl-CoA units have gone through the citric acid cycle too, the grand total is around 106 net ATP per molecule — the molecular reason a gram of fat carries about 9 kcal against carbohydrate's 4: more reduced carbon-hydrogen bonds per gram means more electrons to hand to oxygen. Protein's amino acids are deaminated (the amino group stripped off as ammonia, ultimately excreted as urea via the liver's urea cycle) and their carbon skeletons feed into glycolysis or the citric acid cycle at various entry points — which is why protein is a serviceable but clumsy fuel: the body has to dispose of nitrogen it never needed to burn.

One further point ties the accounting together. ATP itself is not a store of energy in any meaningful sense — the whole body contains only about 250 g of it at any instant, roughly enough to power a few seconds of hard effort, and it is recycled at an astonishing rate: a resting adult turns over something on the order of their own body mass in ATP every day, and a hard-working athlete several times that. ATP is a currency in circulation, not a bank balance, which is why fuel supply must be continuous and why the pathways above are regulated moment to moment rather than run flat out. That regulation is largely allosteric: phosphofructokinase, the committed step of glycolysis, is inhibited by ATP and citrate and stimulated by AMP, so the pathway automatically speeds up precisely when the cell's energy charge falls and slows when it is full. The same logic governs the entry of fat into mitochondria, where malonyl-CoA — a signal that fat synthesis is under way — blocks the carnitine shuttle, ensuring the cell does not burn and build fat simultaneously.

sections.heading: Fed and Fasted: How Hormones Decide Which Fuel Gets Burned
sections.body:
Which of the pathways above actually runs at full tilt at any given moment is not left to chance — it is switched by two pancreatic hormones acting in opposition, and the switch has hard numeric limits worth knowing.

Within minutes of a carbohydrate-containing meal, rising blood glucose triggers the pancreatic beta cells to secrete insulin, which opens GLUT4 glucose transporters in muscle and fat cells, activates glycogen synthase so the liver and muscles pack incoming glucose into glycogen, and suppresses fat breakdown so fat cells store rather than release fatty acids. Glycogen storage is not unlimited: the liver holds roughly 80–120 g (enough to buffer blood glucose for about 12–24 hours of fasting) and skeletal muscle holds a much larger 300–400 g, but muscle glycogen is landlocked — muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase, so it can only burn its own glycogen locally and can never export glucose back into the blood to feed the brain.

As hours pass without food, falling glucose flips the switch: the pancreatic alpha cells secrete glucagon, which breaks liver (not muscle) glycogen back down to glucose and turns on gluconeogenesis — synthesis of new glucose from lactate, glycerol and amino-acid carbon skeletons. Once liver glycogen runs low, typically after roughly a day of fasting, fat becomes the dominant fuel, and the liver starts converting acetyl-CoA it can't fully burn (because oxaloacetate, the citric acid cycle's entry gate, is busy feeding gluconeogenesis) into ketone bodies — acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetone — which the brain, unable to burn fatty acids directly, can use as a substitute fuel once levels rise high enough, typically after 2–4 days of fasting or on carbohydrate intake sustained below roughly 20–50 g/day.

You can watch this whole system's output without opening a cell, because the ratio of CO2 produced to O2 consumed — the respiratory quotient (RQ) — shifts with fuel choice: pure carbohydrate oxidation gives RQ = 1.0, pure fat oxidation gives RQ ≈ 0.7 (fat is oxygen-poor per carbon, so more inhaled O2 is needed per CO2 exhaled), and a mixed diet sits around 0.8–0.85 at rest. Metabolic carts used in exercise-physiology labs measure exactly this ratio through a mouthpiece to tell, non-invasively, which fuel tank a person is currently drawing down.

Two practical corollaries follow. First, the size of the liver glycogen tank explains the sharp weight loss reported in the first few days of any low-carbohydrate diet: each gram of stored glycogen is bound to roughly 3 g of water, so depleting 400 to 500 g of total glycogen sheds one and a half to two kilograms of body mass that is water, not fat, and it returns the moment carbohydrate does. Second, the fact that the brain cannot burn fatty acids directly — they do not cross the blood-brain barrier in useful quantity — is exactly why ketone bodies exist as a distinct fuel class. Without them, prolonged fasting would force the body to cannibalise muscle protein at a rate of several hundred grams a day to supply the brain with glucose, and survival time without food would be measured in days rather than the weeks that are actually observed. Ketoadaptation cuts that protein loss by roughly three quarters.

sections.heading: Equipment You'll Actually Need to Watch Your Own Metabolism at Work
sections.body:
The reason a domestic experiment can reveal genuine metabolic behaviour is that two of the switches described above surface directly in fluids you can sample at home. Blood glucose is the readout of the insulin-glucagon balance, and consumer meters measure it with real electrochemistry rather than a proxy: a drop of blood wicks onto a strip whose electrode is coated with glucose oxidase or glucose dehydrogenase, the enzyme oxidises glucose and passes electrons to a mediator, and the meter converts the resulting microampere current into a concentration. Accuracy is regulated but not laboratory grade — the ISO 15197 standard demands only that 95 percent of readings fall within 15 percent of a reference value, so a reading of 6.0 mmol/L honestly means somewhere near 5.1 to 6.9. That is ample for seeing the shape of a curve and useless for splitting hairs between two readings a few tenths apart, which is why the method below relies on peak height and return time rather than single values.

Ketone measurement has a similar caveat worth understanding before trusting it. Urine strips detect acetoacetate by a nitroprusside reaction that turns pink to purple, but urine reflects what the kidney discarded some time ago rather than the blood right now, and the body's dominant circulating ketone is actually beta-hydroxybutyrate, which those strips do not detect at all. A blood ketone meter measures beta-hydroxybutyrate directly and is correspondingly more informative, at several times the cost per test.

Weighing food to the gram matters because portion estimation by eye routinely errs by 30 to 50 percent, and an unknown carbohydrate dose produces an uninterpretable curve. Finally, used lancets are contaminated sharps: they must go into a rigid, lidded container, never loose into household waste where a collection worker's hand will find them.
ingredients: A digital kitchen scale accurate to 1 g (any basic model from a kitchen-supply or home-goods store) — needed to weigh food to a known carbohydrate content rather than guess.

An over-the-counter blood glucose meter with lancing device, lancets and test strips (sold without a prescription in the diabetes-testing aisle of any pharmacy) — the single most informative tool here.
Urine ketone test strips (same pharmacy aisle) or, for more precision, a blood ketone meter that uses a second type of test strip — used to detect the ketogenesis threshold described above.
A simple stopwatch or your phone's timer, to hold consistent intervals between readings.
A notebook or a free food-tracking phone app with a nutrition database, to log exact grams of carbohydrate, protein and fat eaten.
A bathroom scale and a cloth tape measure — optional, but useful context for tracking energy balance over weeks.

A rigid single-use sharps disposal container (a proper one from a pharmacy, or any hard-sided plastic bottle with a lid) — required for safe lancet disposal; never put used lancets loose in household trash.

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Testing Your Own Glycemic Response and Fuel-Switching Threshold
sections.body:
The design of what follows is deliberately borrowed from the standard oral glucose tolerance test used in clinics, but scaled down and made observational rather than diagnostic. A fixed 50 g carbohydrate dose is used because it is large enough to produce a clear rise in almost anyone yet well below the 75 g load of the formal clinical test, and because holding the dose constant is what makes two different foods comparable — vary the dose and vary the food at once and the comparison means nothing. The sampling times cluster early, at fifteen-minute intervals through the first hour, because that is where the peak occurs in most people; spacing them evenly across two hours would routinely miss it.

The safety boundary here is firm and not negotiable. Anyone with diagnosed diabetes, a history of hypoglycaemia, an eating disorder, pregnancy, or any condition or medication affecting blood sugar should not improvise a fast or a carbohydrate challenge without their doctor's explicit guidance and an agreed safe glucose range. For everyone else the stopping rule is simple: dizziness, shakiness, sweating, confusion or feeling unwell means eat immediately, regardless of what the meter says. A curve is not worth a fainting episode, and no result obtained here diagnoses anything.
steps: On a normal morning, fast for at least 8 hours (water only), then wash your hands and take a fasting blood glucose reading with the meter; write down the number and the exact time.

Weigh out a food containing exactly 50 g of available carbohydrate (about 65 g of dry white rice before cooking, or check a package label and do the arithmetic) and eat it within 5 minutes, alone, with no added fat or fiber-heavy sides that would slow absorption.
Take a fingerstick glucose reading at 15, 30, 45, 60, 90 and 120 minutes after the first bite, logging each value with its exact timestamp.

Plot the six points on graph paper or a spreadsheet; note the peak value, the time it occurred, and whether the 120-minute value has returned close to your fasting baseline — this curve is a rough personal glycemic-response profile.

On a separate day, repeat steps 1–3 with a different 50 g-carbohydrate food that differs in fiber or processing (a whole apple with skin instead of rice, say) and compare peak height and time-to-return between the two curves — this is the glycemic-index effect made visible on your own meter.

To observe the fasted-state switch, pick a day with no other obligations and extend an overnight fast to 16–18 hours, taking a glucose reading and a ketone reading every 3–4 hours; stop the fast and eat immediately if you feel dizzy, shaky, unwell, or your glucose reads below your doctor-confirmed normal range.

Note the clock time at which ketone strips first show a trace (light pink/purple) rather than reading negative — this marks, approximately, the point where liver glycogen has run low enough that ketogenesis has switched on, consistent with the 12–24 hour range described above.

Dispose of every used lancet and test strip in the sharps container, never loose in the trash, and keep all sessions logged in one place so you have a written personal record of both curves to refer back to.

guides.title: Food Preservation — Canning, Drying, Salting & Curing
guides.summary: The physics and microbiology of making food last: water activity, pH, thermal death curves, the acid/low-acid divide that governs botulism risk, plus step-by-step procedures with real temperatures, times, brine concentrations and salt ratios for canning, drying, salting, curing and smoking.

sections.heading: Why food spoils — the four hurdles
sections.body:
Food degrades along four independent routes, and a preservation method that blocks one does nothing about the others. The first is microbial growth: bacteria, yeasts and moulds consuming the food, souring it, and in some cases producing toxins that outlast the organism itself. The second is enzymatic action by the food's own enzymes, still active after harvest or slaughter — polyphenol oxidase browning a cut apple within minutes, lipases splitting fats into free fatty acids that taste rancid, pectinases turning a frozen strawberry to slurry. The third is purely chemical: atmospheric oxygen attacking unsaturated fats and pigments, which is why a dried food kept in a clear jar on a windowsill fades and goes stale even though nothing is growing in it. The fourth is physical damage — insects, rodents, freezer burn, bruising and crushing.
Preservation works by taking away what microbes need to grow. The hurdle concept, formulated by Lothar Leistner, holds that several modest obstacles stacked together beat one extreme obstacle, and give a better-tasting product besides. Salami is not safe because it is very salty, very dry, very acidic or very smoky; it is safe because it is all four, modestly.
Water activity, written aw, is the first hurdle. It is the ratio of the water vapour pressure above the food to that above pure water at the same temperature, a dimensionless number between 0 and 1.00. It measures available water rather than total water, which is why honey at roughly 17 per cent water by mass is nonetheless microbiologically inert: the sugar binds the water so tightly that little is free. Most spoilage bacteria stop below aw 0.91, Staphylococcus aureus manages 0.86, most yeasts stop at 0.88 and most moulds at 0.80, while extreme osmophilic yeasts and xerophilic moulds persist down to about 0.61. Honey sits near 0.60, dried grain 0.60 to 0.65, jam 0.80 and hard salami 0.82 to 0.86.
Acidity is the second hurdle. pH is the negative base-10 logarithm of the hydrogen-ion concentration in moles per litre, so each whole unit is a tenfold change. Below pH 4.6 Clostridium botulinum cannot grow or produce toxin at all, and that single number governs every canning decision.
Temperature is the third. Between 5 and 60 degrees Celsius — the danger zone — pathogens multiply fastest, some doubling every 20 minutes. Below 5 degrees growth slows greatly, and below minus 18 it effectively stops, but cold arrests rather than kills; a thawed food resumes spoiling from where it left off, with the added bonus of cell damage that releases nutrients.
Oxygen and chemical inhibitors are the fourth. Vacuum packing stops moulds and aerobic bacteria, while nitrite, smoke phenols, organic acids, spices and the competitive microbes of a healthy fermentation suppress others. Here lies the trap that kills people: removing oxygen removes the aerobes but actively favours anaerobes, and C. botulinum is a strict anaerobe. A vacuum-sealed low-acid food at room temperature is not preserved, it is incubated. Never rely on one hurdle alone.

sections.heading: The botulism divide: acid vs low-acid foods
sections.body:
Clostridium botulinum is a spore-forming, strictly anaerobic bacterium present in soil and freshwater sediment worldwide, which means it is on the outside of essentially every vegetable ever harvested. Its vegetative cells die readily at ordinary cooking temperatures, but its spores are among the most heat-resistant structures in biology and survive boiling at 100 degrees Celsius for hours. Sealed into a jar of low-acid food and left at room temperature, those spores find exactly what they need — no oxygen, no competition, near-neutral pH, moisture — and germinate, producing botulinum neurotoxin. It is the most poisonous substance known, lethal to an adult in quantities of well under a microgram, and it causes descending flaccid paralysis beginning with double vision and difficulty swallowing and ending in respiratory failure. Crucially, it produces no reliable smell, taste or visible sign. The toxin, unlike the spore, is destroyed by boiling for 10 minutes, which is the basis of the standing recommendation to boil home-canned low-acid food before serving.
The rule that follows divides all canning in two. High-acid foods, at pH 4.6 or below, include fruits, jams, pickles, properly fermented sauerkrauts and tomatoes with added acid. These can be safely processed in a boiling-water bath at 100 degrees Celsius, because C. botulinum cannot grow at that acidity whatever survives the heat; only yeasts, moulds and lactobacilli need killing, and boiling does that comfortably. Low-acid foods, above pH 4.6, include every vegetable — beans, corn, carrots, potatoes, greens — all meat, poultry, fish and seafood, all soups and stocks, and plain tomatoes, which are genuinely borderline at pH 4.2 to 4.9 depending on variety and ripeness. These require a pressure canner reaching 116 to 121 degrees Celsius at 10 to 15 psi gauge pressure. There is no home substitute. A boiling-water bath, an oven, a microwave, a dishwasher, an open-kettle hot fill, or an electric multicooker without a specifically validated canning programme cannot make low-acid canned food safe, and no amount of care with the rest of the procedure compensates.
Acidification moves a food across the line. To can tomatoes safely, add one tablespoon of bottled lemon juice, which has a standardised acidity that fresh lemons do not, or a quarter teaspoon of citric acid, per pint jar of about half a litre; double both for quart jars. Pickling brines should use vinegar of at least 5 per cent acetic acid, diluted no more than one to one with water, giving a finished product below pH 4.6 throughout, not merely on average.
The thermal death of spores follows first-order kinetics: log10(N0/N) = t / D_T, where N0 and N are the initial and surviving spore counts, t is minutes held at temperature, and D_T is the decimal reduction time, the minutes at temperature T needed to kill 90 per cent of the population. For C. botulinum spores D at 121 degrees is about 0.21 minutes. Commercial sterility of low-acid food demands a twelve-D process, twelve successive tenfold reductions — 12 × 0.21, roughly 2.52 minutes at 121 degrees at the coldest point inside the jar. Published processing times run 20 to 100 minutes because almost all of that is heat working its way to the jar's centre.

sections.heading: Water-bath canning, step by step
sections.body:
Equipment: deep pot with rack and lid (water must cover jars by 25–50 mm), tested jars free of nicks, NEW flat lids each time (the sealing compound is single-use), screw bands, jar lifter, bubble tool, clean cloths.
1. INSPECT jars — run a fingertip round each rim; discard any with a chip, since it will not seal.
2. WASH jars in hot soapy water and rinse. If the processing time is under 10 minutes, sterilise jars by boiling 10 minutes (add 1 minute per 300 m above 300 m elevation); longer processes sterilise the contents in situ.
3. PREPARE the food to a tested recipe — do not reduce the acid, sugar or vinegar, and do not thicken with flour or extra fat, both of which slow heat penetration.
4. FILL hot jars with hot product, leaving the specified HEADSPACE: 6 mm (¼ in) for jams and jellies, 12 mm (½ in) for most fruits and pickles. Too little headspace and the contents boil out and foul the seal; too much and the air is not driven out.
5. DE-BUBBLE with a plastic tool round the inside, re-check headspace, WIPE the rim with a clean damp cloth (a smear of food or oil ruins the seal), place the lid, and screw the band "fingertip tight" — snug, not forced, so air can escape during processing.
6. PROCESS: lower jars onto the rack in simmering water, cover with 25–50 mm of water, bring to a full rolling boil, and START TIMING ONLY THEN. Typical: strawberry jam 10 min, peach halves in syrup 20–25 min (pints), dill cucumbers 10–15 min.
7. ALTITUDE CORRECTION — water boils cooler as you climb (about 1 °C per 285 m; 100 °C at sea level, 95 °C at 1,500 m, 90 °C at 3,000 m). Add 1 minute of boiling-water processing for each 300 m (1,000 ft) above 300 m, or 5 minutes per 600 m under some tables. For pressure canning, ADD PRESSURE instead: a weighted gauge goes from 10 psi to 15 psi above 300 m.
8. COOL undisturbed 12–24 h on a towel, no draught. Remove bands, test each seal by lifting the jar by the lid edge; a sealed lid is concave and does not flex. Label with contents and date. Store 10–21 °C, dark, bands OFF (a band can mask a failed seal).
DISCARD without tasting any jar that is unsealed, leaking, bulging, spurting on opening, mouldy, cloudy, foul-smelling, or has a lid that flexes. Suspect low-acid jars should be detoxified before disposal by boiling the contents 30 minutes, and the containers disinfected — botulinum toxin is destroyed by heat but the food must never be tasted to "check".

sections.heading: Drying: mathematics, methods and targets
sections.body:
Drying preserves by lowering water activity below the threshold at which microbes can grow, and it is the oldest and least equipment-dependent method there is. Moisture content on a wet basis is calculated as MC per cent = (m_wet − m_dry) / m_wet × 100, where m_wet is the mass before drying and m_dry the bone-dry mass, both in grams. The practical targets are fruit at 15 to 20 per cent, leathery with no moisture beading when a piece is squeezed and torn; vegetables at 5 to 10 per cent, brittle enough to snap; jerky at roughly 15 to 20 per cent, bending and cracking rather than snapping; grain and beans at 12 to 14 per cent, because above 14 per cent both moulds and storage insects thrive; and herbs at about 10 per cent, crumbling between the fingers.
A useful field rule predicts yield before you start: mass lost is approximately the starting mass × (MC_start − MC_end) / (100 − MC_end). Drying 1,000 grams of apple at 84 per cent moisture down to 18 per cent removes 1,000 × (84 − 18) / (100 − 18), about 805 grams of water, leaving roughly 195 grams of fruit. That four-to-one shrinkage is worth knowing before committing a harvest to trays.
Sun drying needs air above 30 degrees Celsius, relative humidity below about 60 per cent, and moving air; racks half a metre off the ground, food in a single layer, netting against insects, and everything brought under cover each night so dew does not undo the day's work. It suits grapes, tomatoes, chillies and apricots. A solar dryer — a glazed collector box feeding a shaded drying chamber — reaches 55 to 70 degrees and protects colour and vitamin C far better, because the food itself stays out of direct ultraviolet light. An electric dehydrator runs fruit at 57 to 60 degrees for 6 to 16 hours, vegetables at 52 to 55 degrees for 4 to 12 hours, herbs at only 35 to 40 degrees for 2 to 4 hours since higher heat drives off the volatile oils that are the point of the herb, and jerky at 63 to 68 degrees. An oven works at its lowest setting with the door propped 25 to 50 millimetres so vapour can escape; a closed oven simply steams the food.
Pre-treatment matters more than most people expect. Blanching vegetables — steam for 3 to 5 minutes or boil for 2 to 3, then straight into ice water — deactivates enzymes that would otherwise keep degrading colour, flavour and vitamins for months in the jar even with no microbe present. Light fruits dipped for five minutes in ascorbic acid solution, one teaspoon of powdered vitamin C or 1,500 milligrams of crushed tablets per 500 millilitres of water, or in lemon juice diluted one to four, resist enzymatic browning. Cut uniformly: 3 to 6 millimetre slices dry evenly, and because moisture must diffuse out through the thickness, drying time scales roughly with the square of it, so doubling slice thickness roughly quadruples the time.
Jerky carries a specific hazard: dehydrator temperatures alone do not reliably kill Salmonella or E. coli O157:H7 in raw meat, because drying surfaces protect the bacteria as they go. Either heat the strips to an internal 71 degrees Celsius in the marinade before drying, or dry first and then post-heat in a 135 degree oven for 10 minutes.
Conditioning is the step most often skipped. After drying, pack loosely into a sealed jar for 7 to 10 days, shaking daily, so residual moisture equalises between wetter and drier pieces; if condensation appears on the glass, everything goes back to the dryer. Then store airtight and opaque with an oxygen absorber or desiccant, labelled and dated. At 15 degrees Celsius expect 6 to 12 months for fruit and vegetables, and many years for properly dried grain sealed with oxygen absorbers.

sections.heading: Salting and brining
sections.body:
Salt preserves by osmosis. Dissolved sodium and chloride ions lower the water activity of the food's liquid phase, and because a microbial cell is separated from that liquid by a semi-permeable membrane, water is drawn out of the cell toward the higher solute concentration outside. The cell shrinks away from its wall — plasmolysis — and either dies or is arrested. As a working figure, water activity falls about 0.005 for each additional 1 per cent salt by weight in the water phase, so a 10 per cent brine phase gives aw around 0.94 and a fully saturated brine around 0.75. Salt also selects rather than merely kills: lactic acid bacteria tolerate salt better than most spoilage organisms, which is why a correctly salted vegetable ferments instead of rotting.
Brine strength is expressed two ways and confusing them is a common error. Percentage brine by weight is S per cent = mass of salt / (mass of salt + mass of water) × 100. Salometer or salinometer degrees instead express percentage of saturation, where 100 degrees is fully saturated, about 26.4 per cent salt by weight at 16 degrees Celsius. So 10 per cent salt by weight is roughly 38 to 40 degrees salometer. A saturated brine floats a fresh egg high in the liquid; the traditional field test is that an egg showing a coin-sized patch above the surface indicates about 10 per cent salinity. It is a crude gauge and eggs vary with age, so it checks a scale rather than replacing one.
The common ratios each have a reason. Vegetable fermentation such as sauerkraut or kimchi uses 2.0 to 2.5 per cent salt by weight of vegetable, 20 to 25 grams per kilogram of shredded cabbage — enough to select for lactobacilli, not enough to stop them working. Fermented cucumber pickles use a 5 to 8 per cent brine held over the vegetables for 3 to 6 weeks. Dry-salted fish in the klipfish or bacalao tradition is layered with coarse salt at roughly one part salt to three parts fish by weight, pressed, drained daily for about three weeks, then air-dried; it is rehydrated by soaking 24 to 48 hours with several changes of water. A meat brine intended for flavour and juiciness rather than preservation runs 5 to 6 per cent for 1 to 12 hours depending on thickness, and must stay refrigerated throughout.
Salt type matters. Use pure non-iodised salt with no anti-caking agent for fermentation and curing: iodine inhibits some lactobacilli and anti-caking agents cloud the brine. More importantly, measure salt by weight and never by volume, because a tablespoon holds about 18 grams of fine table salt but only 10 to 12 grams of flaky kosher salt — an error approaching twofold, which in a ferment is the difference between a crisp sauerkraut and a soft, mould-topped failure.
Two safety points close the method. Salted foods must stay fully submerged beneath their brine, held down with a weight or a water-filled bag, because anything exposed to air grows mould and kahm yeast regardless of how salty the liquid beneath is. And salt-preserved foods are extremely high in sodium; soaking and rinsing before use removes a good deal of it, but anyone on a sodium-restricted diet should treat these as occasional foods and take clinical advice rather than guess.

sections.heading: Curing and smoking — nitrite, safety and procedure
sections.body:
CURING means preserving meat with salt plus NITRITE (NO₂⁻) or NITRATE (NO₃⁻). Nitrite does three things nothing else does: it specifically inhibits Clostridium botulinum in the anaerobic interior of a sausage or ham; it reacts with myoglobin to form nitrosylmyoglobin, giving cured meat its stable pink colour; and it produces the characteristic cured flavour while retarding rancidity.
CURING SALTS (nomenclature varies by country; read the label and follow the manufacturer's ratio exactly):
• "Cure #1" / "pink salt" / Prague Powder #1 — 6.25% sodium nitrite in 93.75% salt, dyed pink so it is never mistaken for table salt. For cooked or short-cure products: bacon, ham, hot dogs, most smoked sausage. Standard use: 2.5 g per kg of meat (0.25%), delivering about 156 ppm nitrite — the common regulatory maximum.
• "Cure #2" — 6.25% sodium nitrite plus 4% sodium nitrate, for long dry-cured products (salami, coppa, prosciutto) where the nitrate acts as a slow reservoir converted to nitrite by bacteria over weeks or months.
TOXICITY WARNING: sodium nitrite is acutely poisonous. The estimated human lethal dose is in the region of 1 gram of pure nitrite; a few teaspoons of pink curing salt eaten directly can kill by methaemoglobinaemia. Store it labelled, sealed and away from children, and never scale a recipe by eye. Never substitute plain salt for cure or vice versa. Use a scale accurate to 0.1 g.
EQUILIBRIUM (EQ) CURING — the safest home method. Weigh the meat, then calculate every ingredient as a percentage of that mass: typically 2.0–2.75% salt, 0.25% Cure #1, 0–1% sugar, plus spices. Vacuum-seal or bag with all the cure, refrigerate at 2–4 °C, and hold roughly 1 day per 5 mm of thickness plus 2 days (a 50 mm pork belly ≈ 12 days), turning every couple of days. Because the total salt is fixed, the meat cannot become over-salted no matter how long it sits.
SMOKING is a preservation and flavour hurdle, not a substitute for curing:
• COLD SMOKE below 30 °C (86 °F) — flavours and dries but does NOT cook; the meat must already be cured, because these temperatures are squarely in the bacterial growth range.
• HOT SMOKE 60–90 °C — cooks and smokes together; take poultry to an internal 74 °C, whole cuts of pork and beef 63 °C with a 3-minute rest, minced/ground meat 71 °C, fish 63 °C, all measured at the thickest point with a calibrated probe.
Wood smoke deposits phenols and organic acids that are antimicrobial and antioxidant, but also polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons — heavily charred, heavily smoked meat is best eaten occasionally rather than daily. Use hardwoods (oak, hickory, apple, beech); never softwoods (pine, spruce — resinous, acrid), painted, treated, glued or salvaged timber.

sections.heading: Worked example and a preservation decision procedure
sections.body:
Take a concrete case: a 25 kilogram autumn cabbage harvest, no refrigeration, no pressure canner. Cabbage is a low-acid vegetable at about pH 6.0, so plain canning in a boiling-water bath is unsafe and the equipment that would make it safe is unavailable. Two routes remain. Drying works but gives a product few people enjoy. Fermentation is the better answer, because it lowers the pH below 4.6 and in doing so converts the cabbage into a high-acid food, after which water-bath canning becomes legitimate as a second stage.
Working the numbers: trim the head and reserve four intact outer leaves, then core. Net weight after trimming, 22.0 kilograms. Salting at 2.25 per cent gives 22,000 × 0.0225 = 495 grams of non-iodised salt, weighed rather than measured by spoon. Shred to 2 to 3 millimetres, layer with the salt in a food-grade vessel, and massage for about 10 minutes until brine runs freely — that liquid is drawn out of the cabbage by osmosis and is the only brine the ferment needs. Pack tightly to expel air pockets, lay the reserved leaves flat on top as a barrier, weight everything below the brine line, and cover with an airlock or a loose cloth that lets carbon dioxide escape without letting flies in.
Ferment at 18 to 22 degrees Celsius for 3 to 4 weeks. Cooler is slower but gives better flavour, and below 15 degrees it may take two months. The microbiology proceeds in a relay: pH falls from 6.0 to about 4.5 within two or three days as Leuconostoc mesenteroides works and generates the carbon dioxide that displaces the remaining oxygen, then continues to 3.4 to 3.6 as the more acid-tolerant Lactobacillus plantarum takes over. Verify with pH strips or a meter before long storage rather than assuming; a stalled ferment that stops at pH 5 looks and smells broadly similar and is not safe. Then either keep it cold at 0 to 4 degrees, where it holds six months or more, or hot-pack into jars and water-bath process 15 minutes for pints, which is now legitimate precisely because the product has become acid.
The same reasoning generalises into a decision procedure for any food. First, measure or look up the pH. Above 4.6 the only shelf-stable options are pressure canning, drying to aw below 0.85, curing with nitrite, freezing, or acidification and fermentation down below 4.6. Below 4.6, water-bath canning, drying, sugar preserving and fermentation are all available. Second, audit the equipment and energy you actually have rather than the equipment you wish you had: drying needs almost nothing, canning needs jars and sustained heat, freezing needs uninterrupted power for the entire storage life. Third, stack at least two hurdles — salted and dried, acid and canned, cured and cold-smoked and chilled. Fourth, label everything with contents and date, rotate oldest first, and inspect before eating.
The recurring failures are worth naming. Reusing flat canning lids, whose sealing compound is single-use. Inventing recipes or lightening them by cutting vinegar, salt or sugar, all of which are structural rather than culinary. Adding oil, flour, rice, pasta or dairy to canned goods, which slow heat penetration to the jar's centre and are not covered by any tested schedule. Ignoring altitude, which lowers the boiling point roughly 1 degree Celsius per 300 metres. Cooling jars in a draught, which cracks glass by thermal shock. Storing with the screw bands left on, which hides a failed seal. And assuming a sealed lid alone proves safety, which it does not. When any doubt exists, throw it out.

sections.heading: Pressure Canning: The Procedure for Low-Acid Foods, Step by Step
sections.body: Water-bath canning only reaches 100°C (212°F) at sea level — plenty to destroy yeasts, molds and most vegetative bacteria, but Clostridium botulinum spores shrug off boiling water for many hours. Low-acid foods (pH above 4.6 — most vegetables, meats, poultry, seafood) must instead be processed in a pressure canner, which traps steam under pressure to raise the internal temperature to 240°F (116°C) or higher, cutting the time needed for a lethal margin of safety down from many hours to tens of minutes.
steps: Wash jars, lids and rings in hot soapy water; keep jars hot in a low oven or in the canner itself so a cold jar doesn't crack when packed with hot food.

Prepare the low-acid food according to a tested recipe from a trusted current source (a university extension or USDA-style canning guide) — do not substitute jar sizes or ingredient ratios freely, since processing times are calculated for a specific density and headspace.

Pack jars, leaving the headspace the recipe specifies (commonly 1 inch/2.5 cm for most vegetables and meats) — too little headspace can prevent a proper seal, too much can leave food underprocessed at the top.

Wipe the jar rim clean of any food residue with a damp cloth, center a new lid, and screw the ring down to "fingertip tight" — tight enough to hold the lid, loose enough for trapped air to vent during processing.
Add the amount of water the canner manufacturer specifies to the canner base, load the jars onto the rack, and lock the lid.

Vent the canner: let steam escape steadily from the open petcock or weight for a full 10 minutes before pressurizing — this purges air pockets that would otherwise stop the canner reaching a true, even temperature at a given pressure reading.

Bring the canner up to the pressure your recipe specifies for your altitude (commonly 10 psi at sea level on a weighted-gauge canner, rising to 15 psi above roughly 1,000 ft/300 m; dial-gauge canners use different psi bands by altitude, so check your canner's own chart) and start timing only once that pressure is reached and holding steady.

Hold the pressure for the full processing time specified for that food and jar size (commonly 20–90 minutes depending on food density and jar size — pint jars of green beans run around 20 minutes, quart jars of meat can run 75–90 minutes), adjusting heat as needed to keep pressure steady rather than spiking, which risks liquid loss from the jars.

Turn off the heat and let the canner depressurize on its own — never force-cool it or remove the weight early, since a sudden pressure drop can boil the jars' contents violently out through the seal (siphoning) or make the gauge unreliable for the next batch.

Once the gauge reads zero, wait an additional 10 minutes, then unlock and open the lid away from your face, remove jars with a jar lifter, and set them undisturbed on a towel for 12–24 hours before checking that every lid has pulled down and sealed (a sealed lid does not flex when pressed in the center); refrigerate and use promptly any jar that fails to seal.

sections.heading: Freezing and Root-Cellaring: Preservation Without Removing Water
sections.body:
Canning, drying, salting and curing all preserve by putting water out of reach of microbes, pulling water activity below the roughly 0.91 that most spoilage bacteria need. Freezing and cold storage take an entirely different route: they remove no water at all, they simply slow the chemistry and biology until it is negligible. That difference explains their honest limitation — frozen food is not preserved indefinitely, it is preserved for weeks to years, after which oxidation and enzyme action have degraded it even though nothing has grown.
Water expands about 9 per cent in volume on freezing, and the rate of freezing decides how much damage that expansion does. A home freezer at minus 18 degrees Celsius cools slowly, so ice crystals nucleate in few places and grow large and jagged in the spaces between cells, puncturing cell walls as they extend. That is why thawed strawberries collapse into mush and thawed meat weeps, while a commercial blast freezer at minus 40 degrees freezes the same fruit fast enough to nucleate many tiny crystals that leave the cell walls largely intact. The same mechanism explains why refreezing a fully thawed food degrades texture further: it repeats the large-slow-crystal damage a second time. Freezing food in smaller portions and in direct contact with cold metal shelving rather than stacked in an insulated block genuinely improves the result, because it shortens the time spent crossing the zone between about minus 1 and minus 5 degrees where most crystal growth happens.
Freezer burn is not spoilage in the microbial sense. It is sublimation — ice converting directly to vapour from the food's surface into the colder, drier air of the freezer, leaving a pale, dry, leathery patch that is unpleasant but harmless. It is driven entirely by exposed surface area and imperfect sealing, so vacuum-sealed or tightly wrapped food resists it for many months longer than a loosely bagged item. A frost-free freezer, which periodically warms its coils to shed ice, accelerates the process and makes good packaging more important rather than less.
Vegetables destined for the freezer are usually blanched first: a brief plunge into boiling water, commonly 2 to 4 minutes depending on the vegetable and the piece size, followed immediately by an ice-water bath to arrest cooking. This has nothing to do with killing microbes. Its purpose is to destroy the vegetable's own enzymes — peroxidase in particular, whose persistence is the standard laboratory test for adequate blanching — which would otherwise keep degrading colour, flavour, texture and vitamin content for months despite the cold having stopped all microbial growth. Unblanched green beans held a year taste of hay; blanched ones do not.
Root cellaring works in the opposite direction from freezing, holding food just above freezing in a narrow band of temperature and humidity that mimics winter soil. Most root vegetables keep best at 0 to 4 degrees Celsius, 32 to 40 Fahrenheit, with 90 to 95 per cent relative humidity — high humidity matters because the loss is desiccation rather than rot. Potatoes are the notable exception: stored below about 4 degrees their starch slowly converts to sugar, giving a sweet taste and dark frying, so they keep better nearer 7 to 10 degrees. Keep them dark, because light triggers greening and the accumulation of solanine, a bitter toxic alkaloid concentrated just under the skin; cut green flesh away generously or discard the potato. Keep apples and onions away from potatoes as well, since the ethylene apples give off encourages sprouting.

sections.heading: Getting the Gear
sections.body:
Different preservation methods need genuinely different kit, and the reason to understand what each piece does is that several of the substitutions people reach for are unsafe rather than merely inconvenient. The most important distinction on the whole list is between a water-bath canner and a pressure canner. A water-bath canner is only a tall lidded pot with a rack, and it can never exceed the boiling point of water — about 100 degrees Celsius at sea level, lower with altitude — which is adequate for high-acid foods and incapable of sterilising anything else. A pressure canner raises the boiling point by holding the vessel above atmospheric pressure, reaching 116 to 121 degrees at 10 to 15 psi, and that temperature range is the only home method that destroys Clostridium botulinum spores. A generic stovetop pressure cooker is not a substitute: many cannot hold pressure steadily for the required time, their volumes are too small for validated heat-penetration data, and their gauges are not designed for the accuracy the schedules assume.
Jar lids matter for a similar reason. The flat lid's sealing compound deforms permanently against the jar rim as the jar cools and a partial vacuum forms; once deformed it will not reliably seal again, which is why lids are single-use while the screw rings and jars are not. A dial gauge on a pressure canner drifts with age and can read high — meaning the food is under-processed — so many agricultural extension offices test them free or cheaply once a season, and a weighted gauge, which cannot drift because it is a calibrated mass, avoids the problem entirely.
Curing salt deserves particular care. It is a nitrite blend dyed pink specifically so it cannot be mistaken for table salt, because sodium nitrite is toxic in bulk at doses far below what would seem like an ordinary quantity of seasoning. Store it separately, clearly labelled, and weigh it on a scale reading to the gram rather than measuring by spoon.
ingredients: A water-bath canner (a tall lidded pot with a rack) for high-acid foods, and, separately, a pressure canner rated for canning (not a generic stovetop pressure cooker) with a working dial or weighted gauge for low-acid foods.
Wide-mouth and regular-mouth glass canning jars in pint and quart sizes, with new two-piece lids each canning season (the flat lid's sealing compound is single-use) and reusable screw rings.
A jar lifter, a magnetic lid wand, a canning funnel and a plastic (non-metal) headspace/bubble tool — inexpensive canning-utensil sets bundle all four.
A digital probe thermometer and an accurate dial or weighted-gauge pressure canner gauge (some extension offices will test a dial gauge's accuracy for free or low cost).
A food dehydrator with an adjustable thermostat and a fan (or a well-ventilated oven set to its lowest temperature with the door propped) plus mesh drying trays or racks.
A digital kitchen scale, for weighing salt-to-food ratios precisely in brining and curing.

Curing (pink) salt — a sodium nitrite blend sold at butcher-supply or well-stocked kitchen stores, kept away from plain table salt and clearly labeled, since it is toxic in bulk and is formulated to be used only in small, measured curing doses.
A hygrometer/thermometer combo for smokehouses or curing chambers, and food-grade curing chamber space (even a spare refrigerator with a humidity controller) for dry-cured items.
Oxygen absorbers and moisture-proof storage containers (food-grade buckets with gasketed lids, or heavy foil pouches) for finished dried goods.

sections.heading: Recognizing Spoilage and Canning Failures Before They Reach the Table
sections.body:
Every preservation method can fail, and recognising the warning signs matters as much as knowing the procedure — with the sobering caveat that the most dangerous failure of all, botulism, frequently produces no smell, no taste and no visible change whatsoever. Inspection catches most problems, but it cannot be the only safeguard, which is why correct processing in the first place is not negotiable.
A jar that failed to seal is the commonest and most visible failure. Press the centre of a cooled lid: a properly sealed lid stays concave and does not flex or click, because the cooling contents created a partial vacuum that holds it down. An unsealed jar should be refrigerated and used within days, or reprocessed with a fresh lid within 24 hours; it must never simply go on the shelf in hope. A lid that seals and later bulges or pops up, a jar that spurts liquid on opening, or contents that turn cloudy, foamy or show rising gas bubbles are all evidence of active microbial growth after processing. Discard the entire contents without tasting even a fingertip. Pour it out where no person or animal will contact it, and boil any surface it splashed for 10 minutes — botulinum toxin, unlike the spore, is destroyed by boiling. Detoxify suspect jars by boiling them, contents and all, for 30 minutes before disposal if you can do so without splashing.
Flat sour is a subtler failure specific to canned vegetables. The jar seals normally and shows no gas, no cloudiness and no bulge, but a heat-tolerant acid-producing bacterium such as a Bacillus species has survived processing and quietly soured the contents. The only tell is an off, sour smell on opening. That is precisely why any canned low-acid food that smells or tastes even slightly wrong should be discarded rather than tasted again to confirm the impression — the second taste is the dangerous one, and it settles nothing.
Dried foods fail differently. Mould is the main risk, and it almost always traces to inadequate drying or to packaging while still warm, so that condensation forms inside the sealed container overnight and raises local water activity above the threshold. Any mouldy dried food should be discarded entirely rather than having the visible spot cut away, because the fungal hyphae — and any mycotoxins produced, notably aflatoxins on nuts and grain — extend well beyond what the eye can see and are not destroyed by cooking.
Cured and smoked meats announce failure as sliminess on the surface, a grey-green discoloration clearly distinct from the stable pink that nitrite curing produces, or a sharp ammonia-like smell. Each indicates that salt concentration, curing time or temperature control fell short somewhere during a slow process where a single warm week is enough to lose the product. A dry white bloom of Penicillium on a dry-cured salami is normal and desirable; fuzzy black, green or bright orange growth is not. None of these products should ever be tasted as a test, and where a whole batch shared one cure or one chamber, a failure in one piece is a reason to distrust the rest of the batch rather than to salvage it.

guides.title: The Science of Fermentation — Bread, Alcohol, Yogurt & Kraut
guides.summary: How microbes convert sugar into acid, alcohol and gas: the biochemistry of glycolysis and its branches, the organisms responsible, and complete working procedures with weights, temperatures, times and pH targets for sourdough bread, beer and wine, yogurt and cheese, and vegetable ferments.

sections.heading: What fermentation is, chemically
sections.body:
Fermentation is the extraction of energy from an organic substrate without oxygen, in which an organic molecule rather than oxygen serves as the final resting place for the electrons stripped out along the way. Every fermentation begins with glycolysis, formally the Embden-Meyerhof-Parnas pathway, which splits one molecule of glucose (C6H12O6) into two of pyruvate, generating two molecules of ATP and reducing two molecules of the electron carrier NAD+ to NADH in the process. ATP is the cell's usable energy currency and NAD+ is the shuttle that carries electrons about. The whole thing turns on a bookkeeping problem: a cell holds only a small fixed pool of NAD+, and glycolysis stalls dead the moment that pool is fully reduced to NADH. With oxygen available, respiration regenerates NAD+ and extracts roughly 30 to 32 ATP per glucose. Without oxygen, the cell must dump those electrons onto pyruvate or one of its derivatives simply to free the carrier for reuse. That dumping is fermentation, and it yields a meagre two ATP per glucose, which is why fermenting organisms consume sugar so voraciously.

Three branches matter in food. Alcoholic fermentation, run by the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, decarboxylates pyruvate to acetaldehyde plus carbon dioxide, then reduces the acetaldehyde with NADH to ethanol. By mass, 100 g of glucose should theoretically give 51.1 g of ethanol and 48.9 g of carbon dioxide; real yields land at 90 to 95 per cent of that because yeast diverts carbon into building its own cells and into glycerol. Homolactic fermentation, run by Lactobacillus and Streptococcus, simply reduces pyruvate to lactate with essentially no gas and one product, which is what makes yogurt. Heterolactic fermentation, run by Leuconostoc and Lactobacillus brevis through the phosphoketolase pathway, splits the sugar into lactate, ethanol and carbon dioxide together, delivering gas, acid and aroma at once, which is the character of early-stage sauerkraut, kefir and the complexity of sourdough.

A fourth process, acetic fermentation by Acetobacter, is conventionally grouped with the others but is strictly an aerobic oxidation rather than a true fermentation: ethanol plus oxygen gives acetic acid plus water. It makes vinegar deliberately and spoils wine accidentally, by exactly the same chemistry.

Preservation follows directly from all of this rather than being an added trick. Lactic and acetic acids drive the pH below the tolerance of common pathogens, since most food-poisoning organisms cannot grow below about pH 4.6 and Clostridium botulinum in particular is halted there. Ethanol above roughly 12 per cent is itself antimicrobial. Carbon dioxide displaces oxygen from the headspace and blankets the surface. And the fermenting organisms outcompete spoilers directly, consuming the available sugars first and secreting bacteriocins, which are protein antibiotics such as nisin, that kill closely related competitors. A successful ferment is therefore not a sterile food but a food whose microbial population has been deliberately steered toward organisms that are harmless to you and hostile to everything else.

sections.heading: Vegetable ferments — sauerkraut, kimchi, pickles
sections.body:
Lacto-fermentation of vegetables is a spontaneous succession of bacteria already present on the plant's surface, selected by nothing more than salt and the exclusion of air. No culture is added at all. Over the first two days the aerobic and coliform bacteria bloom, then die back as the oxygen is consumed and the first acid appears. From roughly day two to day five, Leuconostoc mesenteroides, a heterolactic organism that tolerates both salt and cold, drives the pH from about 6.0 down to 4.5 while producing carbon dioxide that you can see as bubbling, along with lactate, acetate, ethanol and the aromatic esters that give kraut its character. It self-limits near pH 4.0 because it cannot tolerate its own acid. From about day five to day twenty-one, Lactobacillus plantarum and L. brevis, homolactic and more acid-tolerant, take over and finish the job at pH 3.4 to 3.6 with a total acidity of 1.5 to 2.0 per cent expressed as lactic acid.

The master procedure for sauerkraut turns on one measurement. Shred cabbage to 2 to 3 mm and weigh it, because the salt is a percentage of that weight and nothing else. Add non-iodised salt at 2.0 to 2.5 per cent, which is 20 to 25 g per kilogram of cabbage. Below 1.5 per cent the ferment goes soft and risks spoilage because pectin-degrading organisms are no longer suppressed; above 3 per cent the lactobacilli themselves are inhibited and the result is merely salty. Massage or pound for five to ten minutes until the cabbage releases enough brine to cover itself, then pack it into a jar or crock pressing out every air pocket. Weight everything below the brine with a water-filled bag, a glass disc or a folded outer leaf under a stone, because exposed vegetable means mould. Vent the carbon dioxide with an airlock or by unscrewing the lid daily, or the jar can burst. Hold 18 to 22 degrees C for two to four weeks, tasting weekly, then refrigerate, which nearly halts the ferment and gives six months or more of keeping.

A brine method rather than dry-salting suits cucumbers, carrots, beans and whole vegetables: 3 to 5 per cent brine, meaning 30 to 50 g of salt dissolved per litre of unchlorinated water, poured to cover with everything weighted down, for one to four weeks. Kimchi adds a stage: brine napa cabbage in 5 to 8 per cent salt for two to four hours or dry-salt it for one to two, rinse and drain, then coat with a paste of gochugaru chilli flakes, garlic, ginger, spring onion and often a starch porridge and fish sauce; ferment one to three days at room temperature, then refrigerate for weeks of slow development.

Troubleshooting is mostly pattern recognition. A white, flat, wrinkly film is kahm yeast, harmless and skimmable, but it signals oxygen exposure or too little salt. Fuzzy blue, green, black or pink growth is mould; many traditions skim and continue on a fully submerged brine ferment, but the cautious and correct advice is to discard the batch, because mould hyphae penetrate well below the visible surface and some species produce mycotoxins. Slimy or ropy brine means too warm or too little salt. Soft kraut means the same. A putrid rather than sharply sour smell means discard without tasting.

sections.heading: Dairy ferments — yogurt, kefir and simple cheese
sections.body:
Milk contains ~4.8% lactose (glucose+galactose), ~3.3% protein (80% casein, 20% whey), ~3.5% fat. Lactic acid bacteria convert lactose to lactic acid; as pH falls, the negatively charged casein micelles lose their repulsive surface charge and at their ISOELECTRIC POINT of pH 4.6 they aggregate into a gel — that gel is yogurt, and pressed and drained it is fresh cheese.
YOGURT PROCEDURE:
1. HEAT 1 L milk to 82–85 °C and hold 20–30 minutes (or 90 °C for 5–10 min). This is not sterilisation — it denatures β-lactoglobulin, the main whey protein, so it binds to casein and makes a firmer, less weepy gel. Skipping this step is the single commonest cause of thin yogurt.
2. COOL to 43 °C (110 °F). Above 46 °C the culture is damaged; below 38 °C it sets slowly and sourly.
3. INOCULATE with 2–3% starter: 20–30 mL of live plain yogurt per litre, or a commercial freeze-dried culture. The classic pair is Streptococcus thermophilus and Lactobacillus delbrueckii subsp. bulgaricus, which grow PROTOCOOPERATIVELY: S. thermophilus consumes oxygen and releases formic acid and CO₂ that stimulate L. bulgaricus, which in turn releases amino acids and peptides that feed S. thermophilus. Together they ferment about twice as fast as either alone.
4. INCUBATE undisturbed at 42–45 °C for 4–8 hours until pH ≈ 4.5 and the gel does not flow when the pot is tilted. Then chill promptly; cold arrests acidification. Greek-style yogurt is simply yogurt drained in cloth for 2–6 h, removing whey and roughly doubling protein per spoon.
KEFIR is different: a symbiotic community of ~30–50 species of bacteria and yeasts held in a polysaccharide (kefiran) matrix — the "grains". Add 1–2 tablespoons of grains per 500 mL milk, ferment 18–25 °C for 12–24 h, strain, reuse the grains indefinitely. Because yeasts are involved it is mildly effervescent and contains 0.2–2% ethanol.
SIMPLE ACID CHEESE (paneer/queso fresco): heat 2 L whole milk to 85 °C, remove from heat, stir in 60 mL lemon juice or vinegar a little at a time until the curd separates cleanly from greenish whey (about 1 minute), rest 10 minutes, ladle into cloth, drain 30 minutes, press under a 2 kg weight for 1–2 h. Yield roughly 300–400 g. RENNET cheeses instead use chymosin, an enzyme that cleaves the κ-casein hair layer at a specific bond, letting micelles fuse at near-neutral pH — this gives an elastic curd that can be aged, unlike the crumbly acid curd.
SAFETY: use pasteurised milk unless you know your raw-milk source and accept the documented risk of Listeria, Salmonella, Campylobacter and E. coli O157:H7 — these are particularly dangerous in pregnancy, childhood, old age and immunosuppression. Cultured products are not a treatment for any disease; discuss probiotics with a clinician if you are immunocompromised.

sections.heading: Sourdough — the leavening symbiosis
sections.body:
A SOURDOUGH STARTER is a stable co-culture of wild yeasts (commonly Kazachstania humilis or Saccharomyces cerevisiae) and lactic acid bacteria (Fructilactobacillus sanfranciscensis and relatives), typically at a bacteria:yeast ratio near 100:1. The yeasts make CO₂ (leavening) and ethanol; the bacteria make lactic and acetic acid (flavour, preservation, gluten conditioning). The partnership is stable because the dominant yeast cannot metabolise maltose, which the bacteria prefer to leave alone, while the bacteria tolerate the acidity that excludes competitors.
CREATING A STARTER (7–14 days):
• Day 1: mix 50 g wholemeal flour + 50 g water at ~28 °C in a jar, cover loosely.
• Days 2–4: it may bubble early from Leuconostoc and coliforms and then go quiet and smell odd — this is normal succession, not failure. Once daily, discard all but 50 g and feed 50 g flour + 50 g water.
• Days 5–14: feed twice daily. It is ready when it reliably doubles or triples in 4–8 hours after feeding and smells cleanly yogurty-tangy. pH stabilises at 3.5–4.3.
• Maintenance: at 20–24 °C feed daily at 1:1:1 (starter:flour:water by weight); refrigerated, feed weekly.
BAKER'S PERCENTAGE is the trade's arithmetic: every ingredient is expressed as a percentage of TOTAL FLOUR weight, which is always 100%. A 75% hydration loaf with 1,000 g flour has 750 g water. HYDRATION = water ÷ flour × 100.
BASIC COUNTRY LOAF (makes one ~900 g loaf):
1. Levain: 20 g starter + 100 g flour + 100 g water; 4–8 h at 24 °C until domed and bubbly.
2. Autolyse: mix 800 g bread flour + 200 g wholemeal + 720 g water (72% hydration), rest 45 minutes. During autolyse, flour proteases and the simple hydration of glutenin and gliadin begin building the gluten network with no kneading.
3. Add all the levain and 20 g salt (2% of flour); mix thoroughly.
4. BULK FERMENT 4–5 h at 24–26 °C, folding the dough over itself 4 times at 30–45 minute intervals for the first 2 hours. Bulk is done when the dough has risen 30–50%, is domed and jiggly, and shows bubbles at the edges.
5. Pre-shape, rest 20–30 min, final shape with tension, place seam-up in a floured basket.
6. PROOF 1–2 h at room temperature, or 8–16 h at 4 °C (cold retard develops acetic acid and sour flavour and makes scoring easier).
7. BAKE in a preheated covered Dutch oven at 250 °C for 20 minutes (trapped steam keeps the crust elastic for maximum oven spring), then uncovered at 230 °C for 20–25 minutes to an internal temperature of 96–99 °C.
WHAT THE HEAT DOES: yeast activity peaks then dies near 60 °C; starch GELATINISES from 60–85 °C, absorbing water and setting the crumb; gluten proteins coagulate ~74 °C; the crust browns by Maillard and caramelisation above 150 °C. Sourdough's acidity also degrades phytate, improving mineral availability, and slows starch retrogradation so the loaf stales more slowly.
COMMON MISTAKES: using a starter that is not at peak activity; under-fermenting (dense, gummy crumb) or over-fermenting (slack dough, flat loaf, sour and pasty); adding salt before hydration is complete; opening the oven early; slicing hot bread before the starch has set.

sections.heading: Alcoholic fermentation — beer, wine, cider
sections.body:
Yeast needs FERMENTABLE SUGAR. Fruit supplies it directly; grain supplies starch that must first be converted, which is what malting and mashing do.
MEASURING SUGAR AND ALCOHOL. Specific gravity (SG) is the density of the liquid divided by that of water (1.000). Sugar raises it. Alcohol by volume is estimated as:
  ABV% ≈ (OG − FG) × 131.25
where OG is original gravity before fermentation and FG is final gravity after. Example: OG 1.055, FG 1.010 → (0.045) × 131.25 ≈ 5.9% ABV. Degrees Brix (°Bx) express grams of sucrose per 100 g solution; °Bx ≈ (SG − 1) × 1000 / 4.
WINE / CIDER (simplest route):
1. Crush fruit or press juice. Target OG 1.080–1.095 for wine (≈11–13% ABV), 1.045–1.060 for cider. Add sugar if needed: roughly 17 g of sugar per litre raises SG by 0.007 and gives ~1% ABV.
2. Optionally add potassium metabisulphite at ~50 ppm SO₂ (about ¼ Campden tablet per 4.5 L) and wait 24 hours; this stuns wild organisms so your chosen yeast dominates. Skip it for a spontaneous ferment and accept more variability.
3. Pitch a wine yeast (e.g. Saccharomyces cerevisiae EC-1118 or 71B) at ~1 g per 4–5 L, plus yeast nutrient if the juice is low in nitrogen.
4. PRIMARY ferment 18–24 °C for 5–10 days under a loose cover, then rack (siphon off the sediment) into a vessel with an AIRLOCK — a one-way water seal that lets CO₂ out and keeps oxygen and vinegar bacteria out.
5. SECONDARY 2–8 weeks until the airlock is silent and gravity is stable across three days (FG typically 0.990–1.000 dry).
6. Rack again, age, and bottle. To carbonate, add priming sugar at 6–8 g per litre and bottle in pressure-rated bottles — plain wine bottles or jars can explode.
BEER adds a mash: malted barley (grain germinated then kiln-dried, which develops α- and β-amylase) is milled and steeped in water at 63–70 °C for 60 minutes. β-amylase (optimum ~63 °C) makes maltose and a thinner, drier beer; α-amylase (optimum ~70 °C) leaves more unfermentable dextrins and a fuller body. The sweet wort is then boiled 60 minutes with hops (isomerising alpha acids into bitter iso-alpha acids and sterilising the wort), cooled rapidly to 18–20 °C for ale yeast or 10–12 °C for lager yeast, and fermented 1–2 weeks.
SANITATION is the whole game. Everything touching the cooled wort or juice must be sanitised — an unrinsed no-rinse acid sanitiser, or 1 tablespoon unscented household bleach per 4.5 L water with 10 minutes of contact and a thorough rinse. Clean first, sanitise second; sanitiser does not work through dirt.
SAFETY AND LEGALITY: home brewing and winemaking are legal in many jurisdictions within volume limits, but DISTILLATION is a licensed activity almost everywhere and is dangerous — never distil without legal authorisation. Never ferment in sealed rigid containers (explosion). Never use galvanised, copper-corroded, lead-glazed or non-food-grade plastic vessels. Fermenting vessels release large volumes of CO₂: ferment in a ventilated space, because CO₂ is heavier than air and can pool at floor level in a cellar to asphyxiating concentrations.

sections.heading: Controlling a ferment: the five variables
sections.body:
Every fermentation, whatever the food, is steered by the same five levers, and learning to move them deliberately is the difference between following a recipe and directing a process.

Temperature is the master control. Microbial rates roughly double for every 10 degrees C rise, a relationship expressed as a Q10 of about 2, and they keep doing so until the organism's enzymes begin to denature and the whole thing collapses. Yogurt runs at 42 to 45 degrees C, kefir at 20 to 25, sauerkraut at 18 to 22, ale yeast at 18 to 22, lager yeast at 10 to 12, and a sourdough culture at 24 to 28. Cool ferments run slower but produce more aromatic complexity and fewer harsh fusel alcohols, because the organism has time to metabolise its intermediates properly; hot ferments are fast, blunt and prone to off-flavours.

Salt selects for salt-tolerant lactobacilli while slowing everything down, and it also draws water out of plant cells by osmosis to create the brine in the first place. Use 2.0 to 2.5 per cent for kraut, a 3 to 5 per cent brine for pickles, and 5 to 8 per cent for long fish or olive cures. As a working rule, every additional 1 per cent of salt roughly doubles the fermentation time, so a saltier ferment is not a failed one but a slower one.

Oxygen is unwanted in most food ferments after the first day or two. Submerge solids under brine, fit airlocks, and minimise headspace. The exceptions are instructive: vinegar production requires air because acetic acid bacteria oxidise ethanol using atmospheric oxygen, and koji and tempeh require airflow because the moulds involved are strictly aerobic.

Acidity is the safety metric, not a matter of taste. Verify it with pH strips, whose plus or minus 0.2 accuracy is entirely adequate, or with a calibrated meter. Target 3.4 to 4.0 for sauerkraut and kimchi, 4.2 to 4.6 for yogurt, 3.5 to 4.3 for sourdough, and below 4.6 for any pickle intended to be shelf-stable, because 4.6 is the threshold below which Clostridium botulinum cannot grow. A ferment that has not dropped below pH 4.6 within 48 hours at room temperature has failed to establish and should be discarded rather than nursed along.

Inoculum is the last lever. A ferment may be spontaneous, relying entirely on the microbes already living on the vegetable or fruit, or driven by a defined starter culture. Backslopping, which means adding 2 to 5 per cent of a previous successful batch, is the traditional middle path and a genuinely effective one, because it accelerates acidification through the vulnerable first 24 hours when spoilage organisms still have a chance.

A worked case shows the levers in combination. A kraut fermented at 28 degrees C in a warm kitchen went soft and slightly off within five days. The diagnosis is a temperature high enough to favour pectin-degrading spoilage organisms over L. plantarum, compounded by a salt level probably under 1.5 per cent. The correction for the next batch is to weigh the cabbage precisely, salt at 2.5 per cent, move it to a cellar at 17 to 19 degrees C, and backslop 3 per cent brine from a known-good batch to force the pH below 4.5 within 48 hours. The result was firm, clean kraut at pH 3.5 in three weeks.

sections.heading: Nutrition, benefits and hard safety limits
sections.body:
Fermentation changes the nutritional character of a food in several distinct ways, some of them substantial. It predigests macronutrients: microbial proteases release free amino acids and peptides, so fermented foods are frequently easier to digest than their raw ingredients, and yogurt and aged cheese contain far less lactose than the milk they came from, which is why a great many lactose-intolerant people tolerate them comfortably. It degrades antinutrients, most importantly phytic acid, which binds iron, zinc, calcium and magnesium into complexes the gut cannot absorb; microbial and cereal phytases break it down during sourdough fermentation and during the soaking and fermenting of legumes, measurably improving mineral uptake. Tempeh fermentation reduces the oligosaccharides responsible for flatulence from soybeans. It synthesises vitamins: lactic acid bacteria and yeasts produce folate and riboflavin, and some bacterial ferments such as natto generate vitamin B12. That last point carries a hard caveat, because plant ferments are erratic B12 sources and often contain inactive analogues that occupy the assay without nourishing you; anyone relying on plant foods should use a validated supplement or fortified food rather than trusting a ferment.

Fermentation also removes toxins, and the most consequential example is cassava, whose cyanogenic glycoside linamarin is largely eliminated by grating and fermenting the root for three to five days before cooking. Undetoxified bitter cassava causes acute cyanide poisoning and, on chronic exposure, the irreversible paralytic disease konzo. Finally, fermented foods supply live microbes, commonly 10^6 to 10^9 colony-forming units per gram. The evidence supports modest benefits for certain digestive complaints; claims that fermented foods cure disease are not supported by good evidence and should be treated with scepticism.

Several safety limits are absolute rather than advisory. Never ferment low-acid foods in an oil medium or seal them anaerobically without first acidifying them: garlic in oil and improperly handled fermented fish and marine mammal products are documented botulism vehicles, and botulinum toxin is lethal in microgram quantities. Garlic in oil must be refrigerated and used within days, or acidified. Never ferment meat without a proper nitrite cure and a validated protocol, because charcuterie is the one branch of fermentation where amateur improvisation genuinely kills. Verify pH on anything intended for storage outside a refrigerator. Discard on any sign of fuzzy mould, pink, orange or black growth, sliminess, gas in a product that should not be gassing, or a putrid rather than a sour smell; sour, sharp, yeasty and cheesy are all correct, while rotten, faecal or solvent-like are not, and no amount of skimming corrects them.

People who are pregnant, immunocompromised, very young or very old should be conservative with raw-milk products and homemade ferments in general, since their margin for a contaminated batch is much narrower. This is educational material. Fermented foods interact with medication, notably aged tyramine-rich cheeses with MAO inhibitors and alcohol with a long list of drugs, and with conditions such as histamine intolerance, where even a clean ferment can provoke symptoms. Consult a qualified clinician for personal medical guidance.

sections.heading: Microbial Succession: Who Wins Inside a Jar, and When
sections.body:
A jar of fresh-cut cabbage in 2 per cent brine does not become sauerkraut through the action of a single organism. It runs through a full ecological succession over a few weeks, and the classic mid-twentieth-century food-science studies, most famously Carl Pederson's work on sauerkraut fermentation, mapped a pattern that holds for most vegetable ferments and lets you predict what a jar should look, smell and taste like on any given day.

At the outset the vegetable's natural surface flora is a mixed and unpromising population: assorted coliform-type Enterobacteriaceae, aerobic spoilage bacteria, wild yeasts, and only a small minority of lactic acid bacteria. Two conditions narrow that field before any organism has done much work. Salt at 2 to 3 per cent draws water out of the plant cells by osmosis, creating the brine, while inhibiting most spoilage organisms considerably more than it inhibits the salt-tolerant lactic acid bacteria. And the anaerobic environment inside a submerged, weighted ferment shuts down the strictly aerobic spoilers almost immediately, since they cannot respire without oxygen and have no fermentative fallback.

Into that narrowed field Leuconostoc mesenteroides usually blooms first, a heterofermentative organism producing not only lactic acid but carbon dioxide, ethanol and mannitol. The carbon dioxide physically displaces the last of the oxygen, visible as vigorous bubbling in the first few days, while the acid drives pH from a starting value near 6.5 down toward 4.5. But Leuconostoc is relatively acid-sensitive and is eventually poisoned by its own product. As the pH continues to fall it is progressively out-competed by the far more acid-tolerant Lactobacillus plantarum, a homofermentative organism that converts sugar almost entirely to lactic acid and pushes the pH down further, often to around 3.5.

This final, most acid-tolerant population is what preserves the ferment long term, and it also explains the flavour change you can taste week to week. Finished sauerkraut has a cleaner, sharper sourness than the more complex, faintly effervescent, slightly sweet character of the earlier Leuconostoc-dominated stage, and someone who prefers the younger flavour can simply refrigerate the jar sooner. It also explains why traditional recipes that calmly skim early foam are right to do so rather than treating it as failure: that foam is normal carbon dioxide and yeast activity, and it appears in exactly the window when Leuconostoc is most active. The genuine warning signs are different in kind. A brine that turns ropy or slimy, or one that smells putrid rather than sharply sour, indicates the succession went wrong, usually because the ferment was too warm or too lightly salted for the lactic acid bacteria to seize control before something else did. The practical lesson from the whole sequence is that a vegetable ferment is not managed by intervening in it but by setting the two starting conditions, salt percentage and temperature, that determine which organism inherits the jar at each stage. Once the lid is on, the succession runs itself, and the only useful actions left are keeping the solids submerged and watching the pH fall.

sections.heading: Vinegar and the Second Fermentation: Turning Alcohol Into Acid
sections.body:
Any alcoholic ferment can, if left open to the air, run a second fermentation that converts it into vinegar. This is worth understanding as a single continuous process rather than two unrelated crafts, because it is the same liquid being worked on twice by different organisms with opposite requirements. Yeast fermentation and lactic acid fermentation are both fundamentally anaerobic; vinegar-making flips that requirement entirely. It is strictly aerobic and depends on acetic acid bacteria, most commonly species of Acetobacter.

Acetobacter oxidises ethanol first to acetaldehyde and then to acetic acid, using membrane-bound enzymes positioned on the outer surface of the cell specifically so they can reach dissolved atmospheric oxygen directly. The net reaction is ethanol plus oxygen giving acetic acid plus water, and because oxygen is consumed stoichiometrically, the rate of the whole process is governed by how fast air can reach the liquid rather than by how much alcohol is present. This is why a bottle of wine or hard cider left uncorked in a warm room will turn to vinegar over a few weeks whether you intend it or not, and why sealed, anaerobic storage under an airlock or a full cork is the actual defence against wine going off. There is no special vinegar-specific spoilage organism to guard against; there is only air.

Temperature and starting strength both matter to the outcome. Acetobacter works best somewhere around 25 to 30 degrees C, slowing markedly below about 15. The starting alcohol content should generally sit in the 5 to 10 per cent range: too little and the resulting vinegar is weak and vulnerable to other spoilage organisms, too much and the alcohol itself inhibits the bacteria, which is why fortified wines resist turning. Roughly speaking each percentage point of alcohol converts to about one percentage point of acetic acid, so a 7 per cent cider yields a vinegar near 7 per cent acidity, comfortably above the 5 per cent of typical commercial table vinegar.

A visible by-product of the process is the mother of vinegar, a rubbery translucent mat that forms at the liquid's surface. It is made of cellulose the bacteria secrete in order to hold their own colony precisely at the air-liquid interface, where oxygen is most available. It is harmless and edible, and it is the traditional starter culture used to seed a fresh batch, functioning much as a sourdough starter or a kombucha culture does. Commercial production simply industrialises the same reaction. The slow method is essentially a managed open barrel taking months; the fast method trickles alcohol over a large surface area of wood shavings colonised with acetic bacteria while air is pumped through, maximising oxygen contact and cutting the process to under a day. The chemistry is identical in both cases, and the only variable being optimised is how efficiently oxygen is delivered to the bacteria.
